subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC's capstone unit asks one question for ten chapters: can you add infinitely many numbers and get a finite answer? Before the sums, the terms — sequences, their limits, and the vocabulary that every convergence test will speak.
learning_objectives: Define sequences and compute limits as n → ∞
Apply limit machinery (growth hierarchy, L'Hospital via functions) to sequences
Distinguish a sequence's convergence from the convergence of its series
Identify monotonic and bounded sequences and apply the boundedness theorem
Set the unit's central distinction: terms going to zero versus sums staying finite

sections.title: Sequences and Their Limits
sections.subtitle: Functions on the integers
sections.body:
A sequence is an ordered list a₁, a₂, a₃, ... — a function whose domain is the positive integers, written aₙ = f(n). The sequence CONVERGES to L when lim n→∞ aₙ = L: beyond some index, every term sits arbitrarily close to L. Diverges otherwise — to ∞, to -∞, or by oscillation (aₙ = (-1)ⁿ never settles).

The limit machinery is Unit 1's, evaluated along integers: aₙ = (3n² + 1)/(n² + 5n) → 3 by the degree rule; aₙ = n/2ⁿ → 0 by the growth hierarchy (exponentials beat polynomials); aₙ = (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e by the famous limit. When a limit is genuinely stubborn, pass to the continuous function f(x) and use L'Hospital — if f(x) → L then aₙ = f(n) → L (the converse fails, but the useful direction holds).

Factorials join the hierarchy here, one rung above exponentials: n! eventually dominates every bⁿ, so bⁿ/n! → 0 for every base b. The full dominance ladder — ln n ≪ nᵖ ≪ bⁿ ≪ n! ≪ nⁿ — settles most sequence limits by inspection, and Unit 10 leans on the factorial rungs constantly (the ratio test lives there).

A handful of standard limits to know cold: r ⁿ → 0 for |r| < 1 (the unit's single most important fact); n^{1/n} → 1; (1 + r/n)ⁿ → e^r. These three plus the ladder cover virtually every sequence limit the exam asks.
key_terms: lim n→∞ aₙ = L: terms eventually trapped near L
ln n ≪ nᵖ ≪ bⁿ ≪ n! ≪ nⁿ — factorials now installed
rⁿ → 0 for |r| < 1: the fact the whole unit grows from
boxes: ap_alert

bⁿ/n! → 0 for EVERY b — even 1000ⁿ/n! dies, because factorials multiply by ever-larger factors while bⁿ multiplies by the same b forever. This single fact powers the ratio test's verdict on every exponential-vs-factorial contest in the unit.

sections.title: Sequence vs Series
sections.subtitle: The unit's load-bearing distinction
sections.body:
A SEQUENCE is a list; a SERIES is the sum of a list: Σaₙ = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + ⋯. The series' convergence is defined through its PARTIAL SUMS — the sequence Sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ. If the partial-sum sequence converges to S, the series converges with sum S; otherwise it diverges. Every series question is secretly a sequence question about Sₙ.

The distinction's teeth: the sequence 1/n converges (to zero) — but the series Σ1/n DIVERGES (the harmonic series, certified next chapters). Terms shrinking to zero does NOT make their sum finite: the terms must shrink FAST ENOUGH, and 'fast enough' is exactly what the unit's seven tests adjudicate. Unit 6's improper integrals told the same story (1/x versus 1/x²); the discrete version runs on the same intuition.

Partial sums in action on a telescoping series: Σ 1/(n(n+1)) = Σ[1/n - 1/(n+1)] (partial fractions!). The partial sum collapses: Sₙ = 1 - 1/(n+1) → 1. The series converges to 1 — one of the few series whose exact sum is computable by hand, and the AP's standard telescoping example. (Geometric series, next chapter, are the other exactly-summable family.)

Vocabulary discipline for the whole unit: 'the sequence of terms,' 'the sequence of partial sums,' 'the series' — three different objects, and exam questions name which one they mean. 'Does {aₙ} converge?' and 'does Σaₙ converge?' are different questions with (often) different answers; reading the braces versus the sigma is the first graded act.
key_terms: Σaₙ converges to S iff Sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ → S
1/n → 0 but Σ1/n = ∞: shrinking terms don't guarantee finite sums
Partial-fraction terms collapse: Sₙ computable, limit exact
boxes: ap_alert

'The sequence converges but the series diverges' is a true and tested sentence (aₙ = 1/n). Any answer choice claiming term-convergence implies series-convergence is wrong by this one example — keep the harmonic series loaded at all times.

sections.title: Monotonic and Bounded
sections.subtitle: Convergence without finding the limit
sections.body:
A sequence is MONOTONIC when it always moves one way (increasing or decreasing), and BOUNDED when its terms stay within fixed bars. The Monotone Convergence Theorem: a bounded monotonic sequence converges — it must settle, squeezed between its own direction and its wall, even if the limit's value stays unknown. The theorem certifies existence without computation: the unit's first taste of convergence-without-evaluation.

The standard application: recursively defined sequences. a₁ = 1, aₙ₊₁ = √(2 + aₙ): show the terms increase (an induction-flavored check) and stay bounded above by 2; conclude convergence by the theorem; THEN find the limit by the fixed-point trick — the limit L must satisfy L = √(2 + L), so L² - L - 2 = 0, L = 2. Certify first, then solve: the order matters because the fixed-point equation assumes a limit exists.

Boundedness alone does not suffice ((-1)ⁿ is bounded, oscillates forever); monotonicity alone does not (n increases to ∞). The theorem needs both hypotheses, and the exam's true/false items probe each gap with exactly those counterexamples.

Why the theorem matters ahead: the unit's convergence TESTS mostly certify without summing — 'this converges' with no clue what to. Monotone convergence is the prototype, and it underwrites the integral test's proof (partial sums of positive terms are increasing; bounded by the integral, they converge). The philosophy — existence first, value separately if ever — IS Unit 10.
key_terms: For recursive sequences: certify convergence, then solve L = f(L)
Tests certify convergence without computing sums — the unit's mode
boxes: ap_alert

For recursive sequences, the fixed-point equation L = f(L) is only legal AFTER convergence is certified — applying it to a divergent sequence 'finds' limits that don't exist. The certify-then-solve order is the graded logic.

sections.title: The Unit's Map
sections.subtitle: Ten chapters, one question
sections.body:
The unit's architecture, so the pieces land in slots. Chapters 2-6: CONVERGENCE TESTS for series of constants — geometric and nth-term (ch 2), integral test and p-series (ch 3), comparisons (ch 4), alternating series (ch 5), ratio test (ch 6). Chapters 7-10: POWER SERIES — series with x in them: where they converge (ch 7), Taylor polynomials (ch 8), Taylor series and error (ch 9), and the manipulation calculus (ch 10).

The test-selection skill — WHICH test for which series — is the unit's analog of the integration-technique routing in Unit 6, and the exam tests the routing as much as the executions. A routing preview: geometric form (rⁿ visible) → geometric; terms with n! or bⁿ → ratio; rational-in-n terms → comparison to a p-series; (-1)ⁿ factors → alternating; f(n) with f integrable → integral test. The full decision tree assembles across the chapters and gets drilled in each.

Grading culture in series-land: every convergence claim NAMES its test and VERIFIES the test's hypotheses — 'by the ratio test, since lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = 1/3 < 1' — exactly the theorem-citation discipline of Units 5 and 6. Unjustified verdicts score zero even when correct; the unit is as much about writing proofs-in-miniature as computing.

The stakes, stated once: series questions are roughly 17-18% of the BC exam — the single heaviest topic — including a guaranteed FRQ (usually Taylor-flavored). The ten chapters ahead are the course's highest-density point territory, and the sequence/series distinction this chapter installed is load-bearing under all of it.
key_terms: Tests for constant series (ch 2-6), then power series (ch 7-10)
Form of the term picks the test — the unit's recurring meta-skill
Every verdict cites its test and checks its hypotheses, every time
boxes: ap_alert

Series carry more BC exam weight than any other topic — a guaranteed FRQ plus heavy multiple choice. The justification format ('converges by [test] because [hypothesis check]') is one sentence; written every time, it is worth more points than any single test's mastery.

mcq.explanation: Telescoping: Sₙ = 1 - 1/(n+1) → 1.

mcq.explanation: The Monotone Convergence Theorem: direction plus a wall forces settling.

frq.question:
Consider the sequence aₙ = (3n + 1)/(n + 2) and the series Σₙ₌₁^∞ (3n + 1)/(n + 2).
(a) Find lim n→∞ aₙ.
(b) Determine whether the SERIES converges, with justification previewing the nth-term reasoning: what must be true of a convergent series' terms?
(c) Contrast with bₙ = 1/n: state what its sequence does and what its series does.
rubric: (b) Terms approach 3 ≠ 0: the partial sums grow without bound (adding ≈3 forever): series diverges
The both-directions moral: term-limit 0 is necessary, never sufficient
frq.model_answer: (a) lim aₙ = 3 (equal degrees, leading coefficients 3/1). (b) The series cannot converge: its terms approach 3, so each new partial sum adds nearly 3 — Sₙ grows without bound. (For any convergent series the terms MUST approach zero, since aₙ = Sₙ - Sₙ₋₁ → S - S = 0.) This series diverges. (c) For bₙ = 1/n: the sequence converges to 0, yet the series Σ1/n — the harmonic series — diverges. Together the examples set the unit's central asymmetry: terms → 0 is necessary for convergence but not sufficient; terms ↛ 0 guarantees divergence.

frq.question:
Define a sequence by a₁ = 2 and aₙ₊₁ = √(2 + aₙ).
(a) Compute a₂ and a₃ to three decimals, and conjecture the sequence's behavior.
(b) Given that the sequence is increasing and bounded above by 2, explain why it must converge, naming the theorem.
(c) Find the limit exactly using the fixed-point equation, and explain why that step required (b) first.
rubric: (a) a₂ = 2 = ... √(2+2) = 2: recognizes a₁ = 2 makes it constant — adjust: with a₁ = 1: a₂ = √3 ≈ 1.732, a₃ ≈ 1.932 — accept either treatment with coherent values
(b) Monotone Convergence Theorem: increasing + bounded above ⟹ convergent
Order rationale: the fixed-point equation presupposes a limit exists
frq.model_answer: (a) With a₁ = 2: a₂ = √(2 + 2) = 2 — the sequence is constant at 2 (already at its fixed point); every term is 2.000. The interesting behavior shows from any start below 2 (e.g., a₁ = 1 gives a₂ ≈ 1.732, a₃ ≈ 1.932, climbing toward 2); the conjecture either way: the sequence converges to 2. (b) An increasing sequence bounded above must converge by the Monotone Convergence Theorem — it cannot pass its wall and cannot turn back, so it settles. (c) If aₙ → L, then taking limits in the recursion: L = √(2 + L), so L² = 2 + L, (L - 2)(L + 1) = 0: L = 2 (the negative root is impossible for positive terms). The certification in (b) had to come first: the equation L = f(L) manipulates a limit that must already be known to exist — applied to a divergent recursion it produces phantom 'limits.'

frq.question:
Rank the sequences by eventual size and use the ranking to evaluate three limits.
(a) Order for large n: ln n, n¹⁰⁰, 2ⁿ, n!, nⁿ.
(b) Evaluate lim n→∞ n¹⁰⁰/2ⁿ and lim n→∞ 2ⁿ/n!.
(c) Evaluate lim n→∞ n!/nⁿ, with a one-line reason.
rubric: (b) Both 0: each numerator sits lower on the ladder
frq.model_answer: (a) The dominance ladder: ln n ≪ n¹⁰⁰ ≪ 2ⁿ ≪ n! ≪ nⁿ. (b) n¹⁰⁰/2ⁿ → 0 (polynomials lose to exponentials — 100 rounds of L'Hospital, or the ladder) and 2ⁿ/n! → 0 (factorials multiply by growing factors, exponentials by 2 forever). (c) n!/nⁿ = (1/n)(2/n)(3/n)⋯(n/n): a product of n fractions each at most 1, with the first factor 1/n → 0 — the product is squeezed below 1/n, so the limit is 0. Even factorials lose to nⁿ: the ladder's top rung.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Geometric Series and the nth Term Test
hook: One family of series can be summed exactly, completely, every time: the geometric series, where each term is a fixed multiple of the last. Master its one convergence rule and its one sum formula, then meet the nth Term Test — the unit's quickest divergence detector.
learning_objectives: Recognize geometric series and identify the first term and common ratio
Apply the convergence criterion |r| < 1 and the sum formula a/(1 - r)
Sum geometric series in applied and disguised forms, including repeating decimals
Apply the nth Term Test for divergence, and never as a convergence test
Combine the two tools as the unit's first-pass screening of any series

sections.title: The Geometric Family
sections.subtitle: Fixed-ratio terms, exact sums
sections.body:
A geometric series multiplies each term by a constant ratio r: a + ar + ar² + ⋯ = Σ arⁿ. The partial sum has a closed form — Sₙ = a(1 - rⁿ)/(1 - r) — and its limit hinges entirely on rⁿ: when |r| < 1, rⁿ → 0 (chapter 1's seed fact) and the series converges to S = a/(1 - r). When |r| ≥ 1, the terms refuse to die and the series diverges. One criterion, one formula, no exceptions.

The formula's a is the FIRST TERM as actually written — not necessarily the n = 0 coefficient of a formula. Σₙ₌₂^∞ 3(1/4)ⁿ starts at the n = 2 term: a = 3/16, r = 1/4, sum (3/16)/(3/4) = 1/4. Misreading the starting index is the formula's standard misuse; identify a by writing the first term out, every time.

Worked classics: Σ (2/3)ⁿ from n = 0: a = 1, r = 2/3, sum 3. The repeating decimal 0.717171... = 71/100 + 71/10000 + ⋯: a = 71/100, r = 1/100, sum (71/100)/(99/100) = 71/99 — geometric series turning decimals into fractions, a recurring small question.

Applied dress: a ball dropped from 10 m rebounds to 60% of each fall. Total distance: 10 + 2(6 + 3.6 + ⋯) = 10 + 2·6/(1 - 0.6) = 10 + 30 = 40 m. Bouncing balls, drug accumulation with fractional retention, fractal lengths — the geometric sum is applied mathematics' favorite infinite total, and the AP visits the costume shop regularly.
key_terms: Σarⁿ: converges iff |r| < 1, to a/(1 - r) with a the first written term
a is the series' actual first term — write it out, mind the starting index
Bounces, doses, fractals: the geometric sum in costume
boxes: ap_alert

a/(1 - r) demands a = the FIRST TERM of the series as summed, whatever the index says. For Σₙ₌₃ 5(2/3)ⁿ, a = 5(2/3)³ — not 5. Writing out the first term before the formula is the two-second habit that protects the point.

sections.title: The nth Term Test
sections.subtitle: Divergence on sight
sections.body:
If a series converges, its terms must approach zero (chapter 1's partial-sum argument: aₙ = Sₙ - Sₙ₋₁ → 0). The contrapositive is the nth Term Test for divergence: if lim aₙ ≠ 0 (or fails to exist), Σaₙ DIVERGES. One limit computation, instant verdict — the unit's cheapest test and the right FIRST CHECK on any unfamiliar series.

What the test can never do: certify convergence. lim aₙ = 0 says NOTHING — the harmonic series passes the term-limit check and diverges anyway. The test is a one-way detector: nonzero limit means divergence; zero limit means 'inconclusive, bring a real test.' Treating it as two-way is the unit's most-tested misconception, planted in answer choices at every opportunity.

Applications at speed: Σ n/(2n + 1) — terms → 1/2 ≠ 0: diverges. Σ cos(1/n) — terms → cos 0 = 1: diverges. Σ (-1)ⁿ — terms oscillate, no limit: diverges. Σ (1 + 1/n)ⁿ — terms → e: diverges. Each verdict in one line, each justified 'by the nth Term Test since lim aₙ = [value] ≠ 0.'

The grading sentence has a required shape: name the test, state the nonzero limit. 'Diverges because the terms don't go to zero' without the limit's value is a half-sentence; 'diverges by the nth Term Test because lim aₙ = 1/2 ≠ 0' is the full point. As promised: name-and-verify, every time.
key_terms: lim aₙ ≠ 0 (or DNE) ⟹ Σaₙ diverges — divergence only
Zero term-limit is inconclusive; the harmonic series is the standing witness
Test named, nonzero limit stated: one line, one point
boxes: ap_alert

The nth Term Test NEVER proves convergence — 'converges by the nth term test' is an automatic zero. Its only conclusions are 'diverges' or 'inconclusive,' and the exam plants the misuse as a wrong answer relentlessly.

sections.title: Disguised Geometrics
sections.subtitle: Recognition under costume
sections.body:
Geometric series arrive disguised, and the un-disguising is the tested skill. Exponential rewrites: for Σ 3ⁿ⁺¹/4ⁿ⁻¹, extract the ratio rather than wrestling exponents — each term is (3/4) times the last, and the first term (n = 1) is 3²/4⁰ = 9: a geometric series with a = 9, r = 3/4, sum 9/(1/4) = 36. The reliable method: write two consecutive terms and DIVIDE — the ratio reveals itself regardless of the algebraic costume.

Mixed bases split by linearity: Σ (2ⁿ + 5)/7ⁿ = Σ(2/7)ⁿ + 5Σ(1/7)ⁿ — two geometric series, two sums, added: (2/7)/(5/7) + 5·(1/7)/(6/7) = 2/5 + 5/6 = 37/30. Series split over sums exactly as integrals did; each piece routes to its own family.

The x-powered preview: Σ xⁿ is geometric with ratio x — converging for |x| < 1 to 1/(1 - x). A series of FUNCTIONS, convergent on an interval: the first power series, three chapters early. The geometric family is the seed of the entire power-series half of the unit, which is why its mastery is non-negotiable.

Ratio-extraction also drives the divergent verdicts: Σ (5/4)ⁿ has |r| = 5/4 ≥ 1 — diverges (and the nth Term Test agrees: terms blow up). When both tools apply, cite either; the geometric criterion is self-sufficient for its family.
key_terms: The ratio reveals itself: aₙ₊₁/aₙ, simplified, is r
Mixed numerators decompose into separate geometric series
The geometric series in x: the first power series, interval |x| < 1
boxes: ap_alert
To identify a disguised geometric: compute a₂/a₁ and a₃/a₂. Equal ratios certify the family and HAND you r — no algebra acrobatics on the general term required. Two divisions beat one clever rewrite.

sections.title: The First-Pass Screen
sections.subtitle: Two tools, every series
sections.body:
With two tools installed, the unit's screening protocol begins: given ANY series, (1) check the nth Term Test — terms not dying means done, diverges; (2) check for geometric form — fixed ratio means done, with an exact sum when |r| < 1. The two checks cost seconds and resolve a sizable fraction of exam items outright; everything else proceeds to the heavier tests of chapters 3-6.

The protocol's order matters for efficiency, not correctness: the nth-term check is faster (one limit) and the geometric check more rewarding (exact sums). On multiple choice, scan for both simultaneously: visible rⁿ structure → geometric route; terms with a nonzero limit → instant divergence.

What the screen cannot touch — and the coming chapters can: Σ1/n² (terms die, not geometric: p-series, ch 3); Σ1/(n ln n) (integral test, ch 3); Σ n/(n³ + 1) (comparison, ch 4); Σ(-1)ⁿ/n (alternating, ch 5); Σn!/100ⁿ (ratio test, ch 6 — though the nth Term Test also kills this one: factorial terms blow up). The screen sorts; the specialists finish.

A summing caution to close: only geometric (and telescoping) series yield EXACT sums in this unit. Every other convergent series gets a verdict, not a value — 'converges' with the sum unnamed (until Taylor series attach values to a precious few in chapter 9). Questions asking for 'the sum' are geometric/telescoping flags; questions asking 'converges or diverges' open the full toolkit.
key_terms: nth Term Test first, geometric recognition second — seconds each
Exact sums: geometric and telescoping only; everything else gets a verdict
What the screen passes goes to integral, comparison, alternating, ratio
boxes: ap_alert

'Find the sum' means geometric or telescoping — the only families with computable sums in the unit. If a sum is requested and the series looks like neither, re-examine: a partial-fraction telescope or a disguised ratio is hiding.

frq.question:
A ball is dropped from 12 meters; each bounce returns it to 2/3 of its previous height.
(a) Write the total vertical distance traveled as an expression involving a geometric series.
(b) Compute the total distance exactly.
(c) The ball 'bounces forever' in the model. Explain why the total TIME can also be finite, by exhibiting the time sum's structure (each fall from height h takes √(2h/g) seconds — structure only, no evaluation needed).
rubric: (a) D = 12 + 2·Σₙ₌₁^∞ 12(2/3)ⁿ (each rebound height traveled up then down)
(c) Fall times scale like √h: the time series has ratio √(2/3) < 1 — also geometric, also convergent
Infinite bounces, finite total: the unit's central possibility, instantiated
frq.model_answer: (a) The ball falls 12, then for each n ≥ 1 rises and falls 12(2/3)ⁿ: D = 12 + 2Σₙ₌₁^∞ 12(2/3)ⁿ. (b) The series has first term 12(2/3) = 8 and ratio 2/3: sum 8/(1/3) = 24. D = 12 + 2(24) = 60 meters. (c) Each fall from height h takes time proportional to √h, so successive bounce times scale by √(2/3) per bounce — a geometric sequence with ratio √(2/3) ≈ 0.816 < 1. The time series is geometric and convergent too: infinitely many bounces complete in finite time. Infinite processes with finite totals are exactly what convergent series describe — the ball stops bouncing at a computable instant.

frq.question:
Determine the convergence or divergence of each series; for convergent ones, find the sum.
(a) Σₙ₌₁^∞ (3ⁿ⁺¹)/(4ⁿ)
(b) Σₙ₌₁^∞ (2ⁿ + 5)/(7ⁿ)
(c) Σₙ₌₁^∞ cos(1/n)
rubric: (c) Terms → cos 0 = 1 ≠ 0: diverges by the nth Term Test
frq.model_answer: (a) aₙ₊₁/aₙ = 3/4: geometric with r = 3/4, first term 3²/4 = 9/4. Converges (|r| < 1) to (9/4)/(1 - 3/4) = 9. (b) Split: Σ(2/7)ⁿ + 5Σ(1/7)ⁿ. First piece: a = 2/7, r = 2/7: sum (2/7)/(5/7) = 2/5. Second: 5·(1/7)/(6/7) = 5/6. Total: 2/5 + 5/6 = 37/30. (c) lim cos(1/n) = cos 0 = 1 ≠ 0: the series diverges by the nth Term Test — the terms never stop adding nearly 1.

frq.question:
A patient takes 200 mg of a medication every 24 hours; by each next dose, only 30% of the drug present remains.
(a) Write the amount in the body immediately after the (n+1)st dose as a finite geometric sum.
(b) Find the long-run amount immediately after a dose (the limit).
(c) The safe threshold is 300 mg. Does the long-run post-dose amount stay safe? What about immediately BEFORE a dose?
rubric: Both regimes safe; steady-state reasoning through the geometric limit
frq.model_answer: (a) Each earlier dose has been multiplied by 0.3 per elapsed day: after the (n+1)st dose, Aₙ = 200(1 + 0.3 + 0.3² + ⋯ + 0.3ⁿ). (b) As n → ∞ the geometric sum converges: A = 200/(1 - 0.3) = 2000/7 ≈ 285.7 mg — the steady-state peak. (c) The long-run post-dose level ≈ 285.7 mg stays below the 300 mg threshold ✓. Immediately before a dose, a day's decay has acted: 0.3 × 285.7 ≈ 85.7 mg — the trough. The regimen oscillates forever between ≈85.7 and ≈285.7 mg, safely under the line: an infinite dosing schedule with a finite, geometric ceiling.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Unit 6's improper integrals promised a payoff: the integral test welds series to integrals — Σf(n) and ∫f dx converge or diverge together — and out falls the p-series rule, the unit's single most-used benchmark.
learning_objectives: State and apply the integral test with its three hypotheses
Derive and apply the p-series criterion: convergent iff p > 1
Certify the harmonic series' divergence rigorously
Choose the integral test for f(n) terms with integrable f
Use p-series as the benchmark family for the comparison chapter ahead

sections.title: The Integral Test
sections.subtitle: Rectangles under and over the curve
sections.body:
For a function f that is POSITIVE, CONTINUOUS, and DECREASING on [1, ∞): the series Σₙ₌₁^∞ f(n) and the integral ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx converge or diverge TOGETHER. The proof is a picture: the series' terms are unit-width rectangles that can be hung under the curve (showing Σ from 2 on ≤ ∫) or over it (∫ ≤ Σ) — the sum and the area trap each other, so neither can be finite without the other.

The three hypotheses are graded checkboxes: positive (the trapping needs one-sided rectangles), continuous (the integral needs meaning), decreasing (the rectangles need to fit). The verification sentence — 'f(x) = 1/(x ln x) is positive, continuous, and decreasing for x ≥ 2' — precedes the integral, every time; decreasing is certified by f' < 0 when not obvious.

The showcase the test exists for: Σ 1/(n ln n). The function 1/(x ln x) checks all three boxes (x ≥ 2); the integral ∫₂^∞ dx/(x ln x) = lim [ln(ln x)]₂ᵇ = ∞ — diverges, so the series diverges. No other test in the unit touches this series (comparison benchmarks miss it on both sides) — it is the integral test's signature client, and the u = ln x substitution inside is Unit 6's.

What the test does NOT say: the sum does not EQUAL the integral — only their fates match. Σ1/n² converges (next section) but to π²/6 ≈ 1.645, while ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = 1. Verdicts transfer; values don't.
key_terms: Positive + continuous + decreasing: Σf(n) and ∫f dx share one fate
The hypotheses are graded — certify all three before integrating
The sum and integral converge together but to different numbers
boxes: ap_alert

Σ1/(n ln n) is the integral test's flagship — log-decorated terms that comparisons can't bracket. When a series carries ln n in the denominator, route to the integral test, and bring the u = ln x substitution.

sections.title: The p-Series Rule
sections.subtitle: The benchmark family, certified
sections.body:
Apply the integral test to f(x) = 1/xᵖ and Unit 6's p-test transfers verbatim: Σ 1/nᵖ converges if and only if p > 1. The p-SERIES rule — one boundary, knife-sharp: Σ1/n² converges (p = 2); Σ1/n diverges (p = 1, the harmonic series); Σ1/√n diverges (p = 1/2); Σ1/n^{1.001} converges, barely.

The harmonic series' divergence deserves its certificate displayed: by the integral test, ∫₁^∞ dx/x = ∞, so Σ1/n = ∞ — slowly (the first million terms total ≈ 14.4), but without bound. The slow divergence is why the nth Term Test's insufficiency needed a real proof: the terms die, the sum doesn't, and now we know it rigorously.

Fractional and radical costumes: Σ 1/n√n = Σ1/n^{3/2}: p = 3/2 > 1, converges. Σ n^{-0.99}: diverges. Any pure power of n routes here instantly. The rule is cited BY NAME with the p-value: 'converges as a p-series with p = 3/2 > 1' — the complete one-line justification.

Why the family matters beyond itself: p-series are the measuring sticks the comparison tests (next chapter) hold other series against. A complicated term that BEHAVES like 1/n² for large n inherits convergence by comparison with the p = 2 benchmark. Knowing the family's verdicts cold is the prerequisite for the unit's broadest test.
key_terms: Σ1/nᵖ converges iff p > 1 — the integral test's first dividend
p-series are the comparison tests' measuring sticks
boxes: ap_alert

The p-series justification is one line with the p named: 'p-series, p = 3/2 > 1, converges.' No integral re-derivation needed — the rule may be cited directly, and the exam expects exactly that brevity.

sections.title: Remainder Bounds from Rectangles
sections.subtitle: How far a partial sum can miss
sections.body:
The trapping picture yields a bonus: after summing N terms of a convergent Σf(n), the TAIL (the remainder R_N = Σ_{N+1}^∞ f(n)) is squeezed by integrals: ∫_{N+1}^∞ f dx ≤ R_N ≤ ∫_N^∞ f dx. The leftover rectangles fit under the curve from N on — so the error in stopping at N is bounded by an improper integral you can evaluate.

Worked: Σ1/n², stopped at N = 10. R₁₀ ≤ ∫₁₀^∞ dx/x² = 1/10 — the first ten terms (≈1.5498) sit within 0.1 of the true π²/6 ≈ 1.6449 ✓. And the lower bound ∫₁₁^∞ = 1/11 says the tail is at least 0.0909: the estimate is sharp on both sides.

The 'how many terms' inversion: to estimate Σ1/n² within 0.001, demand ∫_N^∞ dx/x² = 1/N ≤ 0.001: N ≥ 1000. Error tolerances convert to term counts through the tail integral — the unit's first error-control computation, rehearsing the alternating-series and Lagrange bounds ahead.

The AP's appetite here is light but real: remainder-bound items appear as multiple choice ('the error is at most...') with the tail integral as the answer. The deeper value is conceptual — series approximation ALWAYS comes with error bounds in this unit, and the rectangles-under-curves picture is where that discipline starts.
key_terms: ∫_{N+1}^∞ f ≤ R_N ≤ ∫_N^∞ f: the remainder trapped by integrals
Error ≤ ε converts to a term count through the tail integral
Every approximation in Unit 10 ships with a bound — starting here
boxes: ap_alert

Remainder questions use the tail integral STARTING AT N: error after N terms ≤ ∫_N^∞ f(x) dx. Starting the integral at 1 (or at N+1 when the upper bound was asked) flips the answer — match the bound's direction to the question's 'at most/at least.'

sections.title: Routing and the Test's Place
sections.subtitle: When the integral test is the right call
sections.body:
The integral test's niche: terms that are f(n) for an f you can actually INTEGRATE — powers, log-decorated powers, e^{-n}-styles. Its flagship clients: pure p-series (instant by the rule), Σ1/(n ln n) and Σ1/(n(ln n)²) (the log family — divergent and convergent respectively, both by u = ln x), and Σ n e^{-n²} (u = x² inside). If ∫f resists evaluation, the test was the wrong route; comparisons or the ratio test await.

The hypotheses police the boundary: terms that oscillate (not positive) or rise (not decreasing) disqualify. The eventually-decreasing loophole is legal and tested: f decreasing only for x ≥ 5 still works — convergence ignores any finite head of a series, so run the test from 5 and say so. ('The first four terms are a finite number; they cannot change convergence.')

The finite-head principle generalizes beyond this test and deserves its banner: ADDING, REMOVING, OR CHANGING FINITELY MANY TERMS never changes whether a series converges (though it changes the sum). Index shifts (Σ from n = 0 versus n = 3) are convergence-irrelevant; every test in the unit silently uses this.

The routing tree, updated through three chapters: terms ↛ 0 → diverges (nth term). Fixed ratio → geometric, exact sum. Pure power of n → p-series rule. f(n) with integrable f (logs!) → integral test. Next: terms that merely RESEMBLE a benchmark — the comparison tests, where the p-series family earns its keep.
key_terms: p-powers, log-decorated terms, integrable f(n) — where ∫ is doable
Finitely many terms never affect convergence — only the sum
nth term → geometric → p-series → integral; comparisons next
boxes: ap_alert

'Eventually decreasing' satisfies the integral test — state the threshold ('decreasing for x ≥ 3') and invoke the finite-head principle for the skipped terms. The exam accepts the loophole when it is NAMED; silent use looks like an unchecked hypothesis.

mcq.question: Σ 1/n^{3/2}

choices.A: converges as a p-series with p = 3/2 > 1
choices.D: diverges by the nth Term Test

mcq.explanation: Pure power, p = 3/2 over the line. (No exact sum is claimed — p-series verdicts come without values.)

mcq.question: Σ 1/(n ln n) (from n = 2)

choices.A: diverges by the integral test: ∫dx/(x ln x) = ln(ln x) → ∞
choices.D: diverges by the nth Term Test

mcq.explanation: The flagship: u = ln x gives a divergent log-log integral. (D fails: the terms DO go to zero.)

mcq.question: Which series converges?
mcq.explanation: Only p = 1.01 clears the p > 1 bar; the others sit at or below it.

mcq.question: For convergent Σ1/n², the error after summing 20 terms is at most
mcq.explanation: Tail bound: R_N ≤ ∫_N^∞ f. (B is the LOWER bound's value; D underestimates a whole tail by one term.)

mcq.question: The integral test applies to Σf(n) when f is

choices.A: positive, continuous, and decreasing on the tail

mcq.explanation: All three hypotheses, possibly from some index on (the finite-head principle covers the start).

frq.question:
Consider the series Σₙ₌₂^∞ 1/(n(ln n)²).
(a) Verify the integral test's hypotheses for f(x) = 1/(x(ln x)²) on [2, ∞).
(b) Evaluate the improper integral and state the series' verdict.
(c) Contrast with Σ1/(n ln n): same test, different fate — identify exactly where the computation diverges (pun intended).
rubric: (a) Positive and continuous for x ≥ 2; decreasing since numerator constant and denominator increasing (or f' < 0)
(b) u = ln x: ∫du/u² = [-1/u]: lim (1/ln 2 - 1/ln b) = 1/ln 2 — finite: series converges
(c) The ln n version integrates to ln(ln x) → ∞; the squared version to -1/ln x → 0
The exponent on ln is the knife: (ln)¹ diverges, (ln)² converges — a p-test one level down
frq.model_answer: (a) For x ≥ 2: the function is positive (all factors positive) and continuous; it is decreasing because x(ln x)² strictly increases. Hypotheses hold. (b) Substitute u = ln x, du = dx/x: ∫₂^∞ dx/(x(ln x)²) = lim b→∞ ∫_{ln 2}^{ln b} du/u² = lim [−1/u]_{ln 2}^{ln b} = 1/ln 2 — finite. By the integral test, the series CONVERGES. (c) For Σ1/(n ln n), the same substitution yields ∫du/u = ln u → ∞: divergent. The two series differ only in the power on ln, and that power decides everything — a p-test played one logarithmic level down: u-world's Σ1/u versus Σ1/u², the harmonic/p=2 boundary all over again.

frq.question:
Let S = Σₙ₌₁^∞ 1/n².
(a) Compute the partial sum S₄ as a fraction.
(b) Bound the remainder R₄ above and below with tail integrals.
(c) How many terms guarantee an estimate of S within 0.0005? Show the tolerance inversion.
rubric: (b) Tail bounds: R₄ ≤ ∫₄^∞ dx/x² = 1/4 and R₄ ≥ ∫₅^∞ dx/x² = 1/5
Bounds oriented correctly (upper from N, lower from N+1)
frq.model_answer: (a) S₄ = 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 = (144 + 36 + 16 + 9)/144 = 205/144 ≈ 1.4236. (b) The tail after four terms is trapped: ∫₅^∞ dx/x² ≤ R₄ ≤ ∫₄^∞ dx/x², i.e., 1/5 ≤ R₄ ≤ 1/4. (Check against the truth: π²/6 - 205/144 ≈ 0.221, inside [0.2, 0.25] ✓.) (c) Demand R_N ≤ ∫_N^∞ dx/x² = 1/N ≤ 0.0005: N ≥ 2000. Two thousand terms pin the sum within five ten-thousandths — slow convergence made precise, and the tolerance-to-term-count inversion on full display.

rubric: (a) Integral test: ∫x e^{-x²} dx = -e^{-x²}/2: tail integral finite (e^{-1}/2): converges
(b) Numerator between 1 and 3: terms ≥ 1/n... ≥ (1/n); since Σ1/n diverges, the larger series diverges (comparison logic, previewed)
frq.model_answer: (a) f(x) = x e^{-x²} is positive and continuous on [1, ∞), and decreasing there (f' = e^{-x²}(1 - 2x²) < 0 for x ≥ 1). Integral test with u = x²: ∫₁^∞ x e^{-x²} dx = lim [-e^{-x²}/2]₁ᵇ = e^{-1}/2 — finite: the series CONVERGES. (b) The numerator 2 + sin n stays between 1 and 3, so each term is at least 1/n. The series therefore dominates the divergent harmonic series term by term and must itself DIVERGE — the comparison principle the next chapter formalizes, used here in its obvious direction. (c) Σn^{-π} is a p-series with p = π ≈ 3.14 > 1: CONVERGES, by the rule, in one line.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Most series resemble a benchmark more than they match one: n/(n³ + 2) is ALMOST 1/n². The comparison tests convert resemblance into verdicts — directly, by trapping; or by limits, when the trap won't quite close.
learning_objectives: Apply the Direct Comparison Test with correctly-oriented inequalities
Apply the Limit Comparison Test when direct inequalities misbehave
Choose benchmarks by dominant-term analysis of the general term
Recognize when each comparison flavor is the right tool
Write the two tests' distinct justification formats for the exam

sections.title: Direct Comparison
sections.subtitle: Trapped under a roof, pushed over a floor
sections.body:
The Direct Comparison Test (DCT), for series with POSITIVE terms: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges (trapped under a convergent roof); if aₙ ≥ bₙ ≥ 0 and Σbₙ diverges, then Σaₙ diverges (pushed up by a divergent floor). Unit 6's integral comparison, discretized — smaller than finite is finite; bigger than infinite is infinite.

Worked, roof direction: Σ 1/(n² + 3). Since 1/(n² + 3) ≤ 1/n² and Σ1/n² converges (p = 2): converges. Floor direction: Σ 1/(n - 1/2) (n ≥ 1): terms exceed 1/n, the harmonic floor: diverges. The inequality's DIRECTION must match the verdict sought — roofs prove convergence, floors prove divergence, and a comparison pointed the wrong way proves nothing.

The useless directions, named because the exam tests them: aₙ ≤ bₙ with Σbₙ DIVERGENT says nothing (being under an infinite roof is no constraint); aₙ ≥ bₙ with Σbₙ CONVERGENT says nothing (clearing a finite floor is free). Half of all comparison answer-choices are these vacuous cases dressed up; checking 'does my inequality's direction support my verdict?' is the discipline.

The standard inequality toolkit: drop positive terms from denominators (1/(n² + 3) ≤ 1/n²), bound sines and cosines by 1 (|sin n|/n² ≤ 1/n²), enlarge numerators carefully. Clean inequalities exist when the perturbation HELPS the needed direction; when it fights you — the next section's client — limits take over.
key_terms: Under a convergent roof: converges; over a divergent floor: diverges
The inequality must point at the verdict — two of four orientations are vacuous
Drop denominator terms, cap trig by 1: standard moves for clean traps
boxes: ap_alert

Before writing any comparison, say the verdict you EXPECT (from dominant terms), then build the inequality that supports it. Comparisons constructed inequality-first routinely come out vacuous — verdict-first is the workflow.

sections.title: Limit Comparison
sections.subtitle: When the trap won't close
sections.body:
Σ 1/(n² - 3) (n ≥ 2) resists the roof: its terms are slightly BIGGER than 1/n², the wrong side for trapping. The Limit Comparison Test (LCT) rescues resemblance: for positive-term series, if lim n→∞ aₙ/bₙ = c with 0 < c < ∞, then Σaₙ and Σbₙ converge or diverge TOGETHER. Same growth class, same fate — no inequality needed.

Applied: aₙ = 1/(n² - 3), bₙ = 1/n²: ratio n²/(n² - 3) → 1 — finite and positive — so the series shares the p = 2 benchmark's convergence. The LCT trades the DCT's inequality-craft for one limit computation, and on rational-style terms that limit is the degree rule running on autopilot.

Benchmark selection is dominant-term reading: keep each polynomial's top power, discard the rest. n/(n³ + 2): behaves like n/n³ = 1/n² — benchmark Σ1/n², ratio → 1, converges. (3n + 1)/(2n² - n): like 1/n — harmonic benchmark, diverges. √n/(n² + 1): like n^{1/2}/n² = 1/n^{3/2} — converges. The reading is Unit 1's end-behavior analysis, repurposed as benchmark selection.

The justification formats differ and are graded distinctly. DCT: the inequality displayed, the benchmark's fate named ('since 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ 1/n² and Σ1/n² converges (p-series, p = 2), Σaₙ converges by direct comparison'). LCT: the limit computed, its positivity-and-finiteness noted, the benchmark's fate named. Both end at a p-series or geometric citation — the benchmarks must themselves be certified.
key_terms: aₙ/bₙ → c ∈ (0, ∞): the two series share one fate
Top powers only: the general term's large-n silhouette picks bₙ
DCT shows an inequality; LCT shows a limit — each plus the benchmark's certificate
boxes: ap_alert

When the perturbation points the WRONG way for a direct trap (denominators with minus signs: n² - 3), reach for the LCT immediately — the limit doesn't care which side of the benchmark the terms sit on. The minus-sign-in-the-denominator is the routing flag.

sections.title: The Comparison Playbook
sections.subtitle: Worked variety at exam speed
sections.body:
Σ (2ⁿ)/(3ⁿ + 5): dominant terms give (2/3)ⁿ — geometric benchmark. Direct works: 2ⁿ/(3ⁿ + 5) ≤ (2/3)ⁿ, convergent roof: converges. Σ (n + 1)/(n²√n): silhouette n/n^{5/2} = 1/n^{3/2}: LCT ratio → 1: converges. Σ 1/(2ⁿ - n): the minus sign flags LCT against (1/2)ⁿ: ratio 2ⁿ/(2ⁿ - n) → 1: converges. Σ ln n/n: terms EXCEED 1/n for n ≥ 3 — harmonic floor: diverges by DCT.

The ln-decorated cases earn a remark: ln n is eventually bigger than any constant but smaller than any positive power nᵉ. So ln n/n beats the harmonic floor (diverges), while ln n/n³ hides under the roof √n/n³ = 1/n^{5/2} (converges — DCT with ln n ≤ √n, or LCT against 1/n^{5/2}). The wedge-the-log-between-powers move handles the whole family.

Trig-decorated cases split by what the trig does: (2 + cos n)/n² has a numerator trapped in [1, 3] — DCT roof 3/n²: converges. But Σ sin(1/n) has terms RESEMBLING 1/n (since sin x ≈ x for small x): LCT against 1/n with ratio sin(1/n)/(1/n) → 1 — diverges with the harmonic. The small-angle limit from Unit 1, deciding a series fate: the course's threads braiding.

Positivity patrol, the tests' fine print: both comparisons require (eventually) POSITIVE terms. Series with mixed signs route to chapter 5's alternating test or chapter 6's absolute convergence — comparisons on signed series are out of bounds, and the hypothesis is checkable at a glance.
key_terms: Constants ≪ ln n ≪ nᵉ: wedge the log between powers to trap its series
sin(1/n) ~ 1/n: Unit 1's special limit as a benchmark ratio
Comparisons demand positive terms; signed series route elsewhere
boxes: ap_alert

sin(1/n) and 1 - cos(1/n) are LCT clients with Unit 1's special limits as the ratios: sin(1/n) ~ 1/n (diverges); 1 - cos(1/n) ~ 1/(2n²) (converges). The exam loves this braid of old limits and new tests — recognize the small-angle silhouettes.

sections.title: Routing at Mid-Unit
sections.subtitle: Four chapters of tests, one decision tree
sections.body:
The decision tree at the unit's midpoint, consolidated. (1) Terms ↛ 0? Diverges, nth Term Test, done. (2) Geometric form (fixed ratio)? Verdict by |r|, exact sum if convergent. (3) Pure p-power? The rule. (4) Log-decorated, integrable shape? Integral test. (5) RESEMBLES a benchmark (rational-ish, root-ish, trig-decorated)? Comparison — direct if a clean trap exists, limit if not. Two chapters remain to install: alternating series (signed terms) and the ratio test (factorials and exponentials).

Most exam series accept several tests — Σ1/(n²+3) yields to DCT, LCT, AND the integral test — and any correctly-executed route earns full credit. Routing skill is about SPEED, not uniqueness: the fastest correct test wins time for the FRQ. Speed order, roughly: nth-term < p-rule < geometric < DCT/LCT < integral < (ratio, ahead).

Multi-part 'determine convergence' FRQ sets sample across the tree deliberately — one geometric, one comparison, one alternating-or-ratio — auditing the whole toolkit in three parts. Practicing series in mixed batches (not test-by-test) builds the routing reflex the format demands.

The positivity boundary marks the tree's current edge: everything so far assumed nonnegative terms. Chapter 5 crosses it — series whose terms alternate in sign, where cancellation creates convergence that no positive-term test could see, and where the error analysis becomes the cleanest in the whole unit.
key_terms: nth term → geometric → p → integral → comparisons; two tests to come
Multiple tests apply to most series; the fastest correct one is best
Routing is the skill: drill series in shuffled sets, not by chapter
boxes: ap_alert
Multi-series FRQ parts are routing audits: expect one item per branch of the tree. If your answers to all three parts used the same test, re-examine — the exam's design almost never permits it.

mcq.explanation: Under the convergent p = 2 roof. (B's roof is divergent — being under it proves nothing.)

mcq.question: For Σ 1/(n² - 3) (n ≥ 2), the right tool is
mcq.explanation: The minus sign puts terms ABOVE 1/n² — the direct trap fails (B's inequality is false); the limit doesn't care.

mcq.question: Σ n/(n³ + 2) — the dominant-term benchmark and verdict are
mcq.explanation: Silhouette n/n³ = 1/n²; LCT ratio → 1; shares p = 2's convergence.

mcq.question: Σ sin(1/n)

choices.D: diverges by the nth Term Test

mcq.explanation: sin(1/n)/(1/n) → 1: harmonic fate. (D fails — the terms DO go to zero; that's exactly why a real test was needed.)

mcq.question: Knowing 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ with Σbₙ divergent allows the conclusion

choices.A: none — the comparison is vacuous in this orientation

mcq.explanation: Sitting under an infinite roof constrains nothing — the planted vacuous case.

frq.question:
Determine the convergence or divergence of each series, naming the test, the benchmark, and the verifying computation.
(a) Σₙ₌₁^∞ (3 + sin n)/n²
(b) Σₙ₌₂^∞ 1/(n² - n)
(c) Σₙ₌₁^∞ (2ⁿ + n)/(3ⁿ)
rubric: (b) LCT vs 1/n²: ratio n²/(n² - n) → 1: converges (or telescoping/partial fractions)
(c) Split or LCT vs (2/3)ⁿ: ratio → 1 (the n/3ⁿ piece vanishes): converges
frq.model_answer: (a) The numerator sits in [2, 4], so 0 ≤ (3 + sin n)/n² ≤ 4/n². Σ4/n² converges (p-series, p = 2), so by DIRECT COMPARISON the series converges. (b) Benchmark 1/n² (dominant terms): ratio [1/(n² - n)]/[1/n²] = n²/(n² - n) → 1, finite and positive. Σ1/n² converges, so by LIMIT COMPARISON the series converges. (Equivalently: 1/(n²-n) = 1/(n-1) - 1/n telescopes to an exact sum of 1.) (c) Compare the whole term to the geometric benchmark (2/3)ⁿ: the ratio is (2ⁿ + n)/3ⁿ ÷ (2/3)ⁿ = (2ⁿ + n)/2ⁿ = 1 + n/2ⁿ → 1, finite and positive (the n/2ⁿ dies by the dominance ladder). Σ(2/3)ⁿ converges (geometric, r = 2/3), so by LIMIT COMPARISON the series converges.

frq.question:
Consider Σₙ₌₁^∞ ln n/n and Σₙ₌₁^∞ ln n/n³.
(a) Show the first diverges by a direct comparison, stating the index from which your inequality holds.
(b) Show the second converges, using the log wedge ln n ≤ √n (valid for n ≥ 1) or a limit comparison.
(c) State the general principle about where ln n sits among powers, and why it decides both verdicts.
rubric: (a) ln n ≥ 1 for n ≥ 3: terms ≥ 1/n, divergent harmonic floor
(c) Constants ≪ ln n ≪ nᵉ for any ε > 0
The wedge beats the harmonic on one side, hides under p > 1 on the other
frq.model_answer: (a) For n ≥ 3, ln n ≥ ln 3 > 1, so ln n/n ≥ 1/n. The harmonic series diverges, and our terms sit on top of that floor (the finite head n = 1, 2 is irrelevant): Σ ln n/n DIVERGES by direct comparison. (b) Using ln n ≤ √n: ln n/n³ ≤ n^{1/2}/n³ = 1/n^{5/2}. Σ1/n^{5/2} converges (p = 5/2 > 1): the series CONVERGES under that roof. (c) The log lives strictly between constants and every positive power: 1 ≪ ln n ≪ nᵉ. Against 1/n it adds just enough weight to keep the divergence (floor side); against 1/n³ it is feather-light next to any small power, leaving the p > 1 cushion intact (roof side). One wedge, both verdicts.

frq.question:
A student must determine whether Σₙ₌₁^∞ 1/(2ⁿ - n) converges.
(a) Explain why direct comparison with (1/2)ⁿ fails as a trap, despite the resemblance.
(b) Complete the determination with the limit comparison test.
(c) Alternatively, find an index N and a constant c so that 2ⁿ - n ≥ c·2ⁿ for n ≥ N, rescuing a direct comparison. (c = 1/2 works.)
rubric: (a) 2ⁿ - n ≤ 2ⁿ makes the terms ≥ (1/2)ⁿ — above the convergent roof: vacuous direction
(b) LCT: ratio 2ⁿ/(2ⁿ - n) → 1 ∈ (0, ∞); Σ(1/2)ⁿ converges: series converges
(c) n ≤ 2ⁿ⁻¹ for n ≥ 1: 2ⁿ - n ≥ 2ⁿ⁻¹: terms ≤ 2·(1/2)ⁿ — a usable roof
Both rescues coherent; finite-head language where needed
frq.model_answer: (a) Since 2ⁿ - n ≤ 2ⁿ, the terms satisfy 1/(2ⁿ - n) ≥ (1/2)ⁿ — they sit ABOVE the convergent benchmark. Being over a finite floor proves nothing: the direct trap points the vacuous way. (b) Limit comparison with bₙ = (1/2)ⁿ: aₙ/bₙ = 2ⁿ/(2ⁿ - n) = 1/(1 - n/2ⁿ) → 1 (the n/2ⁿ dies by the dominance ladder). The limit is finite and positive, Σ(1/2)ⁿ converges (geometric, r = 1/2), so the series CONVERGES. (c) For n ≥ 1, n ≤ 2ⁿ⁻¹, hence 2ⁿ - n ≥ 2ⁿ - 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 2ⁿ⁻¹ = (1/2)·2ⁿ. Then 1/(2ⁿ - n) ≤ 2·(1/2)ⁿ — under the convergent roof Σ2(1/2)ⁿ: direct comparison rescued. Both routes land the same verdict; the LCT just charged less algebra for the trip.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Alternating Series and the Error Bound
hook: Flip every other sign and divergence can turn to convergence: Σ1/n explodes, but 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - 1/4 + ⋯ settles to ln 2. Cancellation is a force of its own — and it comes with the cleanest error bound in all of calculus.
learning_objectives: Apply the Alternating Series Test with its two hypotheses
Use the Alternating Series Error Bound: |error| ≤ first omitted term
Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence
Classify alternating series into the three possible fates
Run the error bound's tolerance inversions for the exam's standard items

sections.title: The Alternating Series Test
sections.subtitle: Two hypotheses, then convergence
sections.body:
An ALTERNATING series flips sign every term: Σ(-1)ⁿ⁺¹bₙ = b₁ - b₂ + b₃ - ⋯ with bₙ > 0. The Alternating Series Test (AST): if the magnitudes bₙ are (1) DECREASING and (2) approaching ZERO, the series converges. Two checkboxes — bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ and lim bₙ = 0 — and the verdict follows, no benchmark needed.

Why it works is a picture worth keeping: the partial sums hop back and forth — up b₁, down b₂, up b₃ — with ever-shorter hops. The odd partial sums descend, the even ones ascend, each trapped past the other: the hopping point is squeezed into convergence. The shrinking-hop geometry IS the test, and it also delivers the error bound in the next section.

The flagship: the alternating harmonic series Σ(-1)ⁿ⁺¹/n. Magnitudes 1/n decrease to zero ✓✓: converges (to ln 2, a value chapter 9's series will certify). The same magnitudes WITHOUT alternation diverged — cancellation alone rescued the sum. Alternating versions of divergent positive series converging is the chapter's signature phenomenon.

Hypothesis discipline: BOTH boxes are graded. Σ(-1)ⁿ(n+1)/n alternates but its magnitudes → 1 ≠ 0: diverges — by the nth Term Test (the terms themselves don't die), not 'AST failure.' And decreasingness matters when magnitudes wobble: certify with bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ algebraically or via a function's derivative, the integral test's habit reused.
key_terms: Magnitudes decreasing to zero ⟹ the alternating series converges
Partial sums oscillate inward, trapping the limit between consecutive hops
boxes: ap_alert

When an alternating series' magnitudes do NOT go to zero, the right citation is the nth Term Test (terms ↛ 0 ⟹ divergence) — not 'the AST fails.' A failed test never proves divergence; the nth-term argument does.

sections.title: The Error Bound
sections.subtitle: The first omitted term is the whole story
sections.body:
The shrinking-hop picture pays its dividend: when an alternating series (hypotheses holding) is truncated after N terms, the true sum lies between that partial sum and the next one — so the ERROR is at most the next hop: |S - S_N| ≤ b_{N+1}. The first OMITTED term bounds the error. No integrals, no derivatives: read the next term, done.

Worked: approximate Σ(-1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² by its first four terms: S₄ = 1 - 1/4 + 1/9 - 1/16 ≈ 0.7986. The error is at most b₅ = 1/25 = 0.04 — and the true sum π²/12 ≈ 0.8225 indeed sits within 0.04 ✓. Moreover the SIGN of the error matches the first omitted term's sign: the truth lies on the side the next hop points — S₄ underestimates here, since the fifth term is positive.

The tolerance inversion, the exam's standard item: how many terms of Σ(-1)ⁿ⁺¹/n! land within 0.0001 of the sum? Demand b_{N+1} = 1/(N+1)! ≤ 0.0001: (N+1)! ≥ 10000: N + 1 ≥ 8 (since 8! = 40320): N = 7 terms. The inversion is one inequality on the omitted term — the chapter 3 tail-integral inversion's cleaner sibling.

The bound is graded as a cited theorem: 'by the Alternating Series Error Bound, |error| ≤ b₅ = 1/25' — name, inequality, value. And its hypotheses are the AST's: the bound is only legal on series the test certifies, a fine-print line the exam checks by occasionally offering non-decreasing magnitudes.
key_terms: |S - S_N| ≤ b_{N+1}: the first omitted term
The truth sits on the side of the next term's sign
b_{N+1} ≤ ε solves for the required term count
boxes: ap_alert

The error bound is the FIRST OMITTED term — b_{N+1}, not b_N. Off-by-one here flips answer choices, and the exam prices the distinction every time the bound appears. 'Stopped after the 1/9 term' means the bound is the NEXT magnitude, 1/16.

sections.title: Absolute vs Conditional
sections.subtitle: Two grades of convergence
sections.body:
A convergent series Σaₙ converges ABSOLUTELY when Σ|aₙ| also converges — the convergence survives stripping the signs. It converges CONDITIONALLY when Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges — the convergence DEPENDED on cancellation. The alternating harmonic series is conditional (Σ1/n diverges); Σ(-1)ⁿ/n² is absolute (Σ1/n² converges, p = 2).

The classification protocol, two steps in fixed order: (1) test Σ|aₙ| with the positive-term toolkit (p-series, comparisons, ...). Converges? ABSOLUTE — done, since absolute convergence implies convergence. (2) If Σ|aₙ| diverges, test Σaₙ itself (usually by AST). Converges? CONDITIONAL. Diverges? Plain divergence. Three fates, one flowchart.

The implication powering step 1 — absolutely convergent series converge — is a theorem worth respecting: it lets the signed series inherit a verdict from its unsigned shadow, putting the whole positive-term toolkit at signed series' disposal. (Its converse fails: conditional convergence is exactly the counterexample.)

Worked classification: Σ(-1)ⁿ/√n. Step 1: Σ1/√n is a p-series, p = 1/2: diverges — not absolute. Step 2: magnitudes 1/√n decrease to zero: AST converges. Verdict: CONDITIONALLY convergent. The two-step writing — both tests shown, the classification named — is the complete answer format.
key_terms: Σ|aₙ| converges — the verdict survives de-signing; implies convergence
Σaₙ converges only WITH its signs; Σ|aₙ| diverges
Test the absolute series first; AST the original only if needed
boxes: ap_alert

'Determine whether the series converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges' is a fixed three-choice genre with a fixed two-test answer shape: the Σ|aₙ| verdict (with its test), then if needed the AST verdict. Both tests, then the classification word.

sections.title: The Chapter in Exam Position
sections.subtitle: Where alternation shows up and what it pays
sections.body:
Alternating machinery headlines two exam genres. Genre one: the classification item just drilled — multiple choice and FRQ parts both. Genre two: ERROR analysis on Taylor approximations (chapters 8-9): the series for sin, cos, e^{-x}, ln(1 + x), and arctan at positive arguments all alternate, so THIS chapter's error bound is the tool that bounds their truncation errors. The AST bound, not Lagrange, is the intended instrument whenever the relevant series visibly alternates — it is simpler and the exam writes questions expecting it.

A preview of that payoff: chapters 8-9 will build the series for e^{-0.5} = 1 - 0.5 + 0.125 - ⋯, but the error logic is already available — its terms alternate with decreasing magnitudes, so stopping anywhere leaves an error below the next term. The bound transfers to every alternating Taylor evaluation untouched.

The rearrangement curiosity, for honest understanding (the AP tests it only implicitly): conditionally convergent series are fragile — rearranging their terms can change the sum (Riemann's theorem says: to anything). Absolutely convergent series are robust: any rearrangement keeps the sum. 'Conditional' is not a technicality; it marks sums that exist by delicate cancellation.

Mid-unit standings: six tests installed (nth term, geometric, p, integral, comparisons, AST) plus the classification framework. One test remains — the ratio test, the factorial-killer — and with it the toolkit completes and the unit pivots to power series, where every test learned reappears aimed at intervals of x.
key_terms: Alternating Taylor series (sin, cos, e^{-x}...) inherit this chapter's bound
Conditional sums can be rearranged to anything; absolute sums are immovable
Six tests down, ratio to go — then power series
boxes: ap_alert

On Taylor-approximation FRQs, if the series alternates (sin, cos, e at negative arguments), the ALTERNATING bound is the intended error tool — one term, one line. Reaching for Lagrange there is legal but slower and error-prone; the exam writes the numbers to make the AST bound clean.

Bound cited by name; direction from the omitted term's sign

(b) Step 1: Σ1/(n ln n) diverges (integral test: ∫dx/(x ln x) = ln(ln x) → ∞) — not absolute. Step 2: the magnitudes 1/(n ln n) are positive, decreasing, → 0: the AST converges the signed series. CONDITIONALLY CONVERGENT. (c) The magnitudes (2n² + 1)/(3n² + 4) → 2/3 ≠ 0: the terms never approach zero, so the series DIVERGES by the nth Term Test — no classification beyond that is possible.

(c) The contrast is absolute versus conditional convergence: the signs are load-bearing here, since Σ1/n diverges. The alternating harmonic series is CONDITIONALLY convergent — the textbook witness for the whole distinction.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: One test to rule the factorials: compare each term to the one before it, take the limit, and series built from n! and bⁿ surrender instantly. The ratio test completes the toolkit — and next chapter it single-handedly powers the radius of convergence.
learning_objectives: Apply the Ratio Test: L < 1 absolute convergence, L > 1 divergence, L = 1 silence
Execute the ratio algebra for factorials, exponentials, and powers
Recognize when L = 1 makes the test useless and reroute
Use the ratio test through absolute values on signed series
Complete and drill the unit's full test-selection decision tree

sections.title: The Test and Its Logic
sections.subtitle: Eventually geometric
sections.body:
The Ratio Test: compute L = lim n→∞ |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|. If L < 1, the series converges ABSOLUTELY; if L > 1 (or ∞), it diverges; if L = 1, the test says NOTHING. The logic: when consecutive-term ratios settle near L, the tail behaves like a geometric series with ratio L — and geometric fate is decided by |r| against 1. The ratio test is the geometric criterion, generalized to series that are only eventually, approximately geometric.

The showcase: Σ 2ⁿ/n!. Ratio: |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = (2ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!) · (n!/2ⁿ) = 2/(n + 1) → 0 < 1: absolutely convergent. The factorial algebra — (n+1)! = (n+1)·n!, so the n! cancels leaving (n+1) downstairs — is the test's signature move and the chapter's drilled skill.

Divergence side: Σ n!/10ⁿ. Ratio: (n+1)/10 → ∞: diverges (and indeed the terms blow up — the nth Term Test agrees). Factorials upstairs beat any exponential: the dominance ladder's verdict, certified by ratio arithmetic.

The verdict L < 1 delivers ABSOLUTE convergence — the test runs on |aₙ| by construction, so signed series inherit the strongest grade automatically. One computation, the best possible conclusion: part of why the ratio test is the workhorse it is.
key_terms: L = lim|aₙ₊₁/aₙ|: < 1 absolute convergence, > 1 divergence, = 1 silence
(n+1)!/n! = n+1: the move that makes the test compute
L < 1 certifies Σ|aₙ| converges — signed series get the top grade
boxes: ap_alert

Ratio-test algebra is division of consecutive terms: write aₙ₊₁ OVER aₙ as one big fraction, then cancel — factorials by the (n+1)! = (n+1)·n! identity, exponentials by subtracting exponents. The setup line with both terms visible is where the credit (and the accuracy) lives.

sections.title: The L = 1 Blind Spot
sections.subtitle: Where the ratio test sees nothing
sections.body:
Every p-series has ratio limit L = 1: for Σ1/n², the ratio (n/(n+1))² → 1; for the divergent Σ1/n, the ratio n/(n+1) → 1 too. Same L, opposite fates — which is exactly why L = 1 concludes NOTHING. The ratio test is blind to polynomial-rate behavior; its eyes only resolve geometric-rate differences.

The blind spot defines the routing rule: rational functions of n, pure powers, log-decorated powers — anything whose consecutive terms differ by O(1/n) — give L = 1 and waste the computation. Factorials, exponentials, and n-th powers move the ratio AWAY from 1; powers of n alone never do. Glance before computing: no factorial, no bⁿ, no nⁿ — no ratio test.

When L = 1 strikes mid-solution, reroute without ceremony: 'the ratio test is inconclusive; by limit comparison with Σ1/n²...' — naming the silence and switching tests is the graded recovery, not an admission of error. The exam writes items that bait the ratio test into L = 1 precisely to reward students who reroute fast.

For completeness, one relative: the ROOT test (lim |aₙ|^{1/n} against 1) shares the geometric logic and the L = 1 blind spot — useful for nth-power terms like ((n+1)/(2n))ⁿ, and within BC's scope only at the margins. The ratio test covers the exam's actual demands; the root test is a spare key.
key_terms: All p-series ratio to 1: the test cannot see polynomial rates
No factorial/exponential/nⁿ in the term ⟹ don't bother with the ratio test
'Inconclusive; by [other test]...' — naming the silence is the recovery
boxes: ap_alert
'The ratio test gives L = 1, so the series converges' is an auto-zero sentence — L = 1 is SILENCE, never a verdict. The p-series pair (1/n vs 1/n²) is the standing proof both fates survive L = 1.

sections.title: Ratio Drills
sections.subtitle: The algebra at exam speed
sections.body:
Σ n!/nⁿ: ratio = (n+1)!/(n+1)ⁿ⁺¹ · nⁿ/n! = (n+1)·nⁿ/(n+1)ⁿ⁺¹ = (n/(n+1))ⁿ = 1/(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e < 1: converges absolutely. The famous-limit finish — (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e — appearing inside a ratio computation is a BC classic, and the 1/e value is worth recognizing on sight.

Σ (2n)!/(n!)²  (the central binomial coefficients): ratio = (2n+2)(2n+1)/(n+1)² → 4 > 1: diverges. Double-factorial-style cancellations — (2n+2)! = (2n+2)(2n+1)(2n)! — extend the signature move; writing the expansions explicitly prevents the index slips these invite.

The pure powers-of-n family routes to the ratio test only when mixed with factorials or exponentials; alone, Σnⁿ diverges by the nth Term Test before any ratio is needed (its terms blow up). The screening order from chapter 2 still leads: terms ↛ 0 ends the question first.

Signed versions pass through absolute values transparently: Σ(-1)ⁿ 3ⁿ/n! has |ratio| = 3/(n+1) → 0: absolutely convergent, no AST needed. When the ratio test resolves a signed series, it outranks the alternating analysis — absolute convergence is the stronger conclusion and one test cheaper.
key_terms: n!/nⁿ ratios to (n/(n+1))ⁿ → 1/e: famous limit inside the test
Ratio < 1 on |aₙ| settles signed series at the strongest grade directly
boxes: ap_alert

When the ratio involves ((n)/(n+1))ⁿ-type expressions, the limit is 1/e (or e±¹ variants) — NOT 1. Calling it 1 and declaring silence throws away a decisive L = 1/e < 1. The famous limit is the trap's disarm.

sections.title: The Complete Decision Tree
sections.subtitle: Seven tests, one reflex
sections.body:
The unit's toolkit, complete. The tree, in screening order: (1) terms ↛ 0 → DIVERGES, nth Term Test. (2) Geometric form → |r| verdict, exact sum available. (3) Pure p-power → p-rule. (4) Factorials/exponentials/nⁿ → ratio test. (5) Rational-ish or root-ish in n → comparison (limit flavor for messy, direct for clean traps). (6) ln-decorated, integrable → integral test. (7) Alternating signs → two-step classification: absolute toolkit first, AST second. Seven branches; every AP series lands in one.

The tree's order encodes efficiency, not validity — multiple branches often work, and any correct, fully-justified route scores. But the routing reflex (term-form → test) is what survives exam pressure, and mixed-batch drilling is how it builds: shuffle twenty series across all seven branches and route them in under a minute each, executing only afterward.

A worked routing batch, verdicts only: Σn/(n+1): branch 1, diverges. Σ5(0.8)ⁿ: branch 2, geometric with |r| = 0.8 < 1, converges (its exact sum depends on the starting index; the verdict does not). Σ1/n^{1.2}: branch 3, converges. Σn²/2ⁿ: branch 4, L = 1/2, converges absolutely. Σ(n+3)/(n³-2): branch 5, LCT vs 1/n², converges. Σ1/(n(ln n)³): branch 6, converges (u-sub tail finite). Σ(-1)ⁿ/ln n: branch 7, conditional (Σ1/ln n diverges by comparison with 1/n; magnitudes ↓ 0).

With constants-series mastery sealed, the unit pivots: chapter 7 puts x INSIDE the series — Σcₙxⁿ — and asks for which x convergence holds. The answer machine is the ratio test with x in the ratio; the toolkit just built becomes the boundary-checking crew. Power series are where all of this was headed.
key_terms: nth term, geometric, p, ratio, comparison, integral, alternating
Term-form reads to test choice in seconds; execution follows
Power series: the ratio test with x aboard, the toolkit on boundary duty
boxes: ap_alert
Multi-series exam sets are routing audits across the tree. Build the reflex with shuffled batches — route first, execute second — because the exam's time budget pays for recognition, not rediscovery.
