The series DIVERGES — the (5/4)ⁿ engine outruns the polynomial brake, exactly as the ratio test sees.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Power Series and Interval of Convergence
hook: Put x inside the series and a number becomes a function: Σcₙ(x - a)ⁿ. For some x it converges, for others it explodes — and the boundary is always an interval centered at a, with a radius the ratio test computes and endpoints only the old tests can settle.
learning_objectives: Define power series and their centers
Find the radius of convergence via the ratio test on |x|-bearing terms
Test both endpoints separately with the constants-series toolkit
Report intervals of convergence with correct bracket notation
Handle the all-x and center-only edge cases

sections.title: Series with x Aboard
sections.subtitle: Functions defined by convergence
sections.body:
A power series centered at a is Σₙ₌₀^∞ cₙ(x - a)ⁿ = c₀ + c₁(x - a) + c₂(x - a)² + ⋯ — a polynomial that never ends, with x a passenger. For each fixed x it is a constants series that converges or diverges; the set of convergent x's is the series' DOMAIN, and on that domain the series defines a function.

The prototype, from chapter 2: Σxⁿ (center 0, all cₙ = 1) is geometric with ratio x — converging exactly for |x| < 1, to 1/(1 - x). One series, one function, one domain: the template for everything ahead, including the headline fact that the domain came out an INTERVAL centered at the series' center.

That is the structure theorem: a power series' convergence set is always an interval centered at a (possibly just the point a, possibly all of ℝ). The RADIUS of convergence R measures its half-width: absolute convergence for |x - a| < R, divergence for |x - a| > R, and the two endpoints x = a ± R individually undecided — each endpoint its own constants-series question.

Why intervals and never scattered sets: convergence at any point x₀ forces absolute convergence at every x closer to the center (comparison against the geometric decay that convergence at x₀ implies). Convergence spreads inward — so the convergent set has no holes, and the interval shape is forced.
key_terms: Σcₙ(x - a)ⁿ: an unending polynomial, centered at a
Absolute convergence inside |x - a| < R; divergence outside
Working at x₀ forces working at everything nearer the center
boxes: ap_alert
The center is read from the (x - a) factor: Σcₙ(x + 3)ⁿ is centered at a = -3, not 3. The sign misread shifts every subsequent answer; the center is the value making the factor zero.

sections.title: The Ratio Test Finds R
sections.subtitle: x rides through the quotient
sections.body:
Radius-finding is the ratio test with x as cargo: compute L(x) = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| where aₙ = cₙ(x - a)ⁿ — the limit comes out (something)·|x - a| — and demand L(x) < 1. Solving for |x - a| hands over R directly.

Worked: Σ (x - 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ). Ratio: |x - 2|/3 · n/(n+1) → |x - 2|/3. Demand |x - 2|/3 < 1: |x - 2| < 3 — radius R = 3, centered at 2: the open interval (-1, 5), with the endpoints awaiting their own trials.

Factorial coefficients produce the edge cases. Σ xⁿ/n!: ratio |x|/(n+1) → 0 for EVERY x — L < 1 always: R = ∞, the series converges on all of ℝ (this is eˣ's series, chapter 9 will say). Σ n!·xⁿ: ratio (n+1)|x| → ∞ for any x ≠ 0: R = 0, convergence only AT the center. All-x and center-only are real outcomes, produced by factorials' position.

The computation's discipline: keep |x - a| as a block through the algebra (it is a constant as far as n's limit is concerned), and reduce the n-part by the usual cancellation craft. The final inequality |x - a| < R is the deliverable — with the strict inequality marking that endpoints remain open questions.
key_terms: Ratio test with x aboard: solve the resulting |x - a| inequality for R
Factorials downstairs: everywhere; factorials upstairs: center only
Carry it untouched through the n-limit; solve at the end
boxes: ap_alert

The radius computation's answer is an INEQUALITY: |x - 2| < 3. Stopping at 'R = 3' without translating to the interval (-1, 5) — or translating with an arithmetic slip — wastes the computation. Center ± radius, written out.

sections.title: Endpoint Trials
sections.subtitle: Two constants series, tried separately
sections.body:
At x = a ± R, the ratio limit is exactly 1 — silence — and each endpoint becomes a CONSTANTS series for the chapter-2-through-6 toolkit. The trials are independent: one endpoint can converge while the other diverges, and all four include/exclude combinations occur.

The worked example, finished: Σ(x - 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) on (-1, 5). At x = 5: Σ3ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = Σ1/n — harmonic: DIVERGES. At x = -1: Σ(-3)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = Σ(-1)ⁿ/n — alternating harmonic: CONVERGES (conditionally). Interval of convergence: [-1, 5) — square bracket where the trial passed, round where it failed.

The endpoint outcomes follow a readable pattern: coefficients like 1/n produce harmonic-vs-alternating-harmonic endpoints (half-open intervals); 1/n² produces p = 2 at both ends (closed); no n-decay at all (Σxⁿ) leaves both endpoints with non-vanishing terms (open). The coefficient's strength decides how much of the boundary survives.

The full protocol, named for the exam: (1) ratio test for R; (2) write the open interval; (3) test EACH endpoint by substitution, citing the test used at each; (4) report with brackets. Four steps, two of them constants-series work — the unit's first half earning its keep inside its second.
key_terms: Each end is its own constants series; the trials can split
Square where the endpoint converges, round where it diverges
1/n: half-open; 1/n²: closed; no decay: open — the readable pattern
boxes: ap_alert

Endpoint testing is a GRADED STEP with its own points: substitute each endpoint, name the resulting series, cite its test. Intervals reported without the two trials — even when the brackets happen right — leave those points on the table.

sections.title: The Genre at Full Form
sections.subtitle: Interval-of-convergence, exam edition
sections.body:
The interval-of-convergence FRQ part is among BC's most predictable: 'find the interval of convergence of Σ [given series].' The rubric, almost invariant: ratio test set up with consecutive terms shown (1 pt), limit computed with the |x - a| block (1 pt), R and the open interval (1 pt), each endpoint tested and cited (1-2 pts). The four-step protocol IS the rubric.

A second full run, centered off-origin with shifted indexing: Σₙ₌₁^∞ (-1)ⁿ(x + 1)ⁿ/(n²·2ⁿ). Ratio → |x + 1|/2 < 1: center -1, R = 2, open interval (-3, 1). At x = 1: Σ(-1)ⁿ/n² — converges absolutely (p = 2). At x = -3: Σ(-1)ⁿ(-2)ⁿ/(n²2ⁿ) = Σ1/n² — converges. Interval: [-3, 1], closed — the 1/n² coefficients held both ends, as the pattern predicted.

Variants to expect: series in (2x - 1)ⁿ-style blocks (factor to 2ⁿ(x - 1/2)ⁿ: the center hides at 1/2 and the effective ratio doubles); series with only even powers Σcₙx²ⁿ (the ratio test runs on x² — solve |x|² < bound); and 'for what x does the series converge ABSOLUTELY?' (the open interval, before endpoint nuance — except endpoints that converge absolutely join it).

What the interval is FOR: on it, the power series is a function — differentiable, integrable, manipulable, the entire subject of chapters 8-10. Taylor polynomials approximate such functions; Taylor series ARE such functions; and the interval computed here is where all of that is legal. The boundary work of this chapter is the license for everything that follows.
key_terms: Setup, limit, R-and-interval, endpoint trials: four steps, four-plus points
(2x - 1)ⁿ factors to reveal center 1/2 and a rescaled radius
The interval is where the series-as-function calculus of ch 8-10 operates
boxes: ap_alert
For (bx - c)ⁿ blocks, FACTOR OUT b first: (2x - 1)ⁿ = 2ⁿ(x - 1/2)ⁿ — center 1/2, and the 2ⁿ joins the coefficients. Reading the center as 1 (from the unfactored block) is the variant's designed trap.

mcq.question: The power series Σ (x - 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) has center and radius
mcq.explanation: The (x - 2) factor centers at 2; the ratio limit |x - 2|/3 < 1 gives R = 3.

mcq.question: Σ xⁿ/n! converges
mcq.explanation: Ratio |x|/(n+1) → 0 < 1 regardless of x: the factorial downstairs defeats every |x|.

mcq.question: For Σ (x - 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ), the endpoint x = 5 yields the series

choices.A: Σ1/n, divergent — so x = 5 is excluded

mcq.explanation: (5-2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = 1/n: the harmonic series. The right endpoint fails its trial.

mcq.question: A power series centered at 4 converges at x = 7 . It must also converge at
mcq.explanation: Convergence at distance 3 forces (absolute) convergence at every distance under 3: |2 - 4| = 2 < 3 ✓. The others sit at distance ≥ 4 — unknown territory.

mcq.question: The series Σ n!(x - 1)ⁿ converges
mcq.explanation: Ratio (n+1)|x - 1| → ∞ for any x ≠ 1: R = 0, the center-only edge case.

frq.question:
Find the interval of convergence of Σₙ₌₁^∞ (x - 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ), executing the full four-step protocol.
(a) Apply the ratio test and find the radius of convergence.
(b) Test the endpoint x = 5.
(c) Test the endpoint x = -1 and report the interval with correct brackets.
frq.model_answer: (a) |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = [|x-2|ⁿ⁺¹/((n+1)3ⁿ⁺¹)]·[n·3ⁿ/|x-2|ⁿ] = (n/(n+1))·|x-2|/3 → |x-2|/3. Convergence demands |x-2|/3 < 1: |x - 2| < 3 — radius 3, centered at 2, open interval (-1, 5). (b) x = 5: the series becomes Σ3ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = Σ1/n — the harmonic series, divergent (p-series, p = 1). Endpoint excluded. (c) x = -1: Σ(-3)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ) = Σ(-1)ⁿ/n — the alternating harmonic series, convergent by the Alternating Series Test (magnitudes 1/n decrease to zero). Endpoint included. Interval of convergence: [-1, 5).

frq.question:
Find the interval of convergence of Σₙ₌₁^∞ (-1)ⁿ(x + 1)ⁿ/(n²·2ⁿ).
(a) Find the center and radius.
(b) Test both endpoints.
(c) Explain — via the coefficient-strength pattern — why this series kept both endpoints while the previous problem's series kept only one.
rubric: (b) x = 1: Σ(-1)ⁿ/n² converges absolutely; x = -3: Σ1/n² converges: both pass
(c) 1/n² coefficients leave p = 2 series at the ends; 1/n coefficients left harmonic-strength ends
frq.model_answer: (a) The (x + 1) block centers the series at -1. Ratio: (n²/(n+1)²)·|x+1|/2 → |x+1|/2 < 1: R = 2, open interval (-3, 1). (b) At x = 1: Σ(-1)ⁿ·2ⁿ/(n²2ⁿ) = Σ(-1)ⁿ/n² — absolutely convergent (p = 2). At x = -3: Σ(-1)ⁿ(-2)ⁿ/(n²2ⁿ) = Σ(2)ⁿ·.../(n²2ⁿ) = Σ1/n² — convergent. Both endpoints join: interval [-3, 1]. (c) Endpoint series inherit the coefficients' decay: here the 1/n² coefficients leave p = 2 series at both ends — convergent regardless of sign pattern. The previous series' 1/n coefficients left harmonic-strength ends, where only the sign-alternating one survived. Stronger coefficient decay holds more boundary.

frq.question:
Consider Σₙ₌₀^∞ (2x - 1)ⁿ/4ⁿ.
(a) Rewrite the general term to expose the center, and identify it.
(b) Find the radius and interval of convergence (this series is geometric — exploit that).
(c) For x inside the interval, find the SUM of the series as a function of x.
rubric: (b) Geometric with r = (2x-1)/4: |2x-1| < 4: -3/2 < x < 5/2; endpoints give |r| = 1 terms ↛ 0: open interval
Geometric reasoning replaces the ratio test cleanly
frq.model_answer: (a) The term is ((2x - 1)/4)ⁿ — a geometric series in r = (2x - 1)/4. Factoring the block: 2ⁿ(x - 1/2)ⁿ/4ⁿ — the center is x = 1/2. (b) Geometric convergence: |r| < 1 ⟺ |2x - 1| < 4 ⟺ -4 < 2x - 1 < 4 ⟺ -3 < 2x < 5 ⟺ -3/2 < x < 5/2. At the endpoints |r| = 1 and the terms (±1)ⁿ never die: both excluded. Interval: (-3/2, 5/2) — open, as no-decay coefficients predicted. (c) Inside, the geometric sum formula applies: S(x) = 1/(1 - r) = 1/(1 - (2x-1)/4) = 4/(4 - 2x + 1) = 4/(5 - 2x). A power series, summed to a closed-form function — the chapter's whole arc in one line.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Match a function's value, slope, bend, and every higher wiggle at a single point, and a polynomial becomes the function's near-perfect local twin. Taylor polynomials are the bridge from the whole course's derivatives to the unit's infinite series — and the AP's guaranteed series FRQ lives here.
learning_objectives: Construct Taylor polynomials matching derivatives at a center
Write the general Taylor polynomial formula with factorial denominators
Build Maclaurin (centered-at-0) polynomials for the standard functions
Use Taylor polynomials to approximate function values
Compute Taylor polynomials from a table of derivative values

sections.title: Matching Derivatives at a Point
sections.subtitle: The construction principle
sections.body:
A Taylor polynomial approximates f near a center a by MATCHING derivatives there: the polynomial P and the function f are forced to share P(a) = f(a), P'(a) = f'(a), P''(a) = f''(a), and so on up to some order n. Agreeing on value pins the height, on slope the direction, on second derivative the bend — each matched derivative buys a sharper local fit.

The coefficients fall out of the matching. For P(x) = c₀ + c₁(x - a) + c₂(x - a)² + ⋯, differentiating and evaluating at a shows cₖ = f^{(k)}(a)/k! — the factorial appearing because differentiating (x - a)ᵏ k times yields k!. The general Taylor polynomial of order n:

Pₙ(x) = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ [f^{(k)}(a)/k!] (x - a)ᵏ = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) + [f''(a)/2!](x - a)² + ⋯ + [f^{(n)}(a)/n!](x - a)ⁿ.

The first-order polynomial P₁ IS the linearization from Unit 4 — Taylor polynomials are linearization's higher-order siblings, each term a correction the tangent line missed. The factorial denominators are the derivative tower of Units 2-3 (x^k differentiating to k!) cashing in exactly where Unit 2 promised: 'the factorials this unit kept producing are Taylor's coefficients.'
key_terms: Pₙ matches f's first n derivatives at the center a
cₖ = f^{(k)}(a)/k!: the factorial from differentiating (x-a)ᵏ
P₁ is the tangent line; higher terms are its corrections
boxes: ap_alert

The kth coefficient is f^{(k)}(a) DIVIDED BY k! — the factorial is not optional. Writing f''(a)(x-a)² without the 2! is the construction's most common error, and it corrupts every approximation built on it.

sections.title: The Maclaurin Library
sections.subtitle: The five series to know cold
sections.body:
Maclaurin polynomials center at a = 0, and five functions' series are memorization-mandatory — they recur in every series FRQ and unlock the manipulation chapter. eˣ: 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ⋯ (every derivative is 1 at 0). sin x: x - x³/3! + x⁵/5! - ⋯ (odd powers, alternating). cos x: 1 - x²/2! + x⁴/4! - ⋯ (even powers, alternating). 1/(1 - x): 1 + x + x² + ⋯ (the geometric series). ln(1 + x): x - x²/2 + x³/3 - ⋯.

The sin/cos pattern rewards understanding over rote: sine is odd (only odd powers), cosine even, both alternating because their derivative cycles hit -1 every other time. Differentiating sin's series term-by-term yields cos's series — a consistency the manipulation chapter exploits. The structure is the mnemonic.

eˣ's series is the cleanest object in the unit: self-derivative means every coefficient is 1/k!, and substituting -x, 2x, or x² generates e^{-x}, e^{2x}, e^{x²} instantly (chapter 10's substitution trick). It is the series most likely to anchor an FRQ.

The geometric series 1/(1 - x) = Σxⁿ closes the circle to chapter 2: the unit's first series is also a Maclaurin series, and its manipulations (substitute, differentiate, integrate) produce arctan's and ln's series in chapter 10. Five series, memorized as patterns; their derivatives, integrals, and substitutions generate dozens more.
key_terms: eˣ, sin x, cos x, 1/(1-x), ln(1+x): memorization-mandatory
sin odd, cos even, both alternating — structure as mnemonic
Self-derivative, coefficients 1/k!, substitution-friendly: the FRQ favorite
boxes: ap_alert

Memorize the five Maclaurin series as the unit's alphabet — they appear in nearly every series FRQ, and chapter 10's manipulations BUILD on them rather than re-deriving. Time spent here is repaid threefold; the five are non-negotiable.

sections.title: Approximation and Tables
sections.subtitle: Putting polynomials to work
sections.body:
Taylor polynomials approximate by EVALUATION: to estimate f at a point near the center, plug it into Pₙ. e^{0.1} ≈ P₃(0.1) = 1 + 0.1 + 0.01/2 + 0.001/6 ≈ 1.10517 — four terms, five-decimal accuracy, because 0.1 is close to the center 0 and the factorials crush the tail. Closer to the center and higher order both sharpen the estimate (the error analysis is chapter 9).

The table genre is the AP's signature Taylor FRQ: a table gives f(a), f'(a), f''(a), ... at the center, and you ASSEMBLE the polynomial by dividing each by its factorial. Given f(2) = 3, f'(2) = -1, f''(2) = 4, f'''(2) = 12: P₃(x) = 3 - (x-2) + (4/2!)(x-2)² + (12/3!)(x-2)³ = 3 - (x-2) + 2(x-2)² + 2(x-2)³. The construction is pure bookkeeping — derivative over factorial, times the power — and the bookkeeping IS the graded skill.

Approximation-from-table chains the two: build Pₙ from the table, evaluate at the requested point. 'Use P₃ to approximate f(2.1)': substitute x = 2.1 into the assembled polynomial. The factorial denominators and the (x - a) powers must both be right; a table FRQ tests both in one line.

Derivative-recovery runs the genre backward: given a Taylor polynomial, READ a derivative off the coefficient. If the x³ coefficient of f's Taylor polynomial at 0 is 5, then f'''(0)/3! = 5, so f'''(0) = 30. The coefficient-to-derivative inversion (multiply by the factorial) appears on the exam as often as the forward construction.
key_terms: Estimate f(point) by substituting into Pₙ — closer center, higher order, sharper
Assemble Pₙ from tabulated derivatives over factorials — the signature genre
f^{(k)}(a) = k! · (coefficient of (x-a)ᵏ) — read derivatives backward
boxes: ap_alert

To recover a derivative from a Taylor coefficient, MULTIPLY by the factorial: f^{(5)}(0) = 5! · (x⁵ coefficient). The exam asks this as often as the forward build — the coefficient already carries the 1/k!, so undoing it returns the raw derivative.

sections.title: The Genre and What's Next
sections.subtitle: Taylor polynomials on the exam, and the leap to series
sections.body:
The Taylor FRQ's standard anatomy: (a) construct Pₙ (from a formula's derivatives or a table); (b) use it to approximate a value; (c) bound the error (chapter 9's Lagrange or the alternating bound); (d) a manipulation — differentiate/integrate the polynomial, or recognize it as a known series (chapter 10). Parts (a) and (b) are this chapter; the FRQ is guaranteed, and these two parts are its reliable points.

The approximation-quality intuition, made precise next chapter: Taylor polynomials are EXCELLENT near the center and degrade with distance — P₃ for eˣ nails e^{0.1} but misses e^{3} badly. 'Near' is measured against the function's curvature, exactly as linearization's error was; the Lagrange bound (chapter 9) quantifies the degradation.

The conceptual leap ahead: a Taylor POLYNOMIAL stops at order n; a Taylor SERIES never stops — Σₖ₌₀^∞ [f^{(k)}(a)/k!](x - a)ᵏ. For many functions the infinite series doesn't just approximate — it EQUALS the function on an interval (eˣ everywhere, the geometric series on (-1,1)). The polynomial is a truncation of the series; the series is the function itself, spelled in powers.

Where this lands the course: the derivative tower (Units 2-3) supplies the coefficients, the convergence tests (chapters 2-7) certify where the series is valid, the error bounds (chapters 5, 9) measure the truncation, and the manipulations (chapter 10) build a library. Taylor series are the unit's summit — every earlier chapter feeds them — and the next two chapters complete the climb.
key_terms: Construct, approximate, bound the error, manipulate — four parts
Excellent close to a, degrading with distance and curvature
Pₙ truncates at order n; the series runs forever and often EQUALS f
boxes: ap_alert

The series FRQ is guaranteed on the BC exam, and parts (a)-(b) (construct and approximate) are its most reliable points — no convergence subtleties, just derivative-over-factorial bookkeeping and one substitution. Bank these before attempting the error and manipulation parts.

mcq.question: The third-degree Taylor polynomial for f at a = 0, given f(0) = 1, f'(0) = 2, f''(0) = 6, f'''(0) = 12, is
The Maclaurin series for cos x is
mcq.explanation: Even powers, alternating signs — cosine is even. (B is sine; D is eˣ.)

mcq.question: Using P₂(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 for eˣ, the estimate of e^{0.2} is
If the Maclaurin series of f has x⁴ coefficient equal to 7, then f^{(4)}(0) =
mcq.explanation: f^{(4)}(0) = 4!·7 = 24·7 = 168 — multiply the coefficient by the factorial.

mcq.question: The first-degree Taylor polynomial P₁ is the same as

choices.A: the linearization (tangent line) of f at the center

mcq.explanation: P₁(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) — Unit 4's linearization exactly.

frq.question:
A function f has these derivative values at x = 1: f(1) = 4, f'(1) = -2, f''(1) = 6, f'''(1) = -24.
(a) Write the third-degree Taylor polynomial P₃ for f about x = 1.
(b) Use P₃ to approximate f(1.2).
(c) Given additionally that the coefficient of (x-1)⁴ in f's Taylor polynomial is 5, find f⁗(1).

Let f(x) = ln(1 + x).
(a) Compute f(0), f'(0), f''(0), f'''(0) and write the third-degree Maclaurin polynomial.
(b) Use it to approximate ln(1.1).
(c) Identify the pattern and write the general Maclaurin series for ln(1 + x).

The Maclaurin series for eˣ is 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ⋯.
(a) Write the third-degree Maclaurin polynomial for eˣ and use it to approximate √e = e^{0.5}.
(b) Write the Maclaurin series for e^{-x²} by substitution, through the x⁴ term.
(c) Use your answer to (b) to find the value of the 8th derivative of g(x) = e^{-x²} at 0, via its coefficient.
rubric: (c) The x⁸ term: substituting gives (-x²)⁴/4! = x⁸/24, coefficient 1/24; g^{(8)}(0) = 8!/24 = 1680
frq.model_answer: (a) P₃(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6. e^{0.5} ≈ 1 + 0.5 + 0.125 + 0.0208 = 1.6458 (true √e ≈ 1.6487 — the omitted x⁴/24 term ≈ 0.0026 accounts for most of the gap). (b) Substitute -x² into the eˣ series: e^{-x²} = 1 + (-x²) + (-x²)²/2! + (-x²)³/3! + ⋯ = 1 - x² + x⁴/2 - x⁶/6 + ⋯. (c) The x⁸ term comes from (-x²)⁴/4! = x⁸/24: its coefficient is 1/24. Since that coefficient equals g^{(8)}(0)/8!, we get g^{(8)}(0) = 8!/24 = 40320/24 = 1680 — substitution sidesteps eight rounds of differentiation entirely.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Taylor Series and the Lagrange Error Bound
hook: When does the infinite Taylor series actually EQUAL its function — not approximate, equal? The Lagrange error bound answers it, measuring exactly how far a truncated series can stray. It is the unit's most feared formula and, drilled, one of its most mechanical.
learning_objectives: Define Taylor series and the condition for series-equals-function
State and apply the Lagrange error bound for the remainder
Choose the max-derivative bound M correctly on the relevant interval
Run tolerance inversions: how many terms for a target accuracy
Choose between the Lagrange and alternating error bounds

sections.title: When Series Equals Function
sections.subtitle: The remainder must vanish
sections.body:
A function's Taylor series Σ [f^{(k)}(a)/k!](x - a)ᵏ is, at each x in its interval of convergence, a NUMBER — but is that number f(x)? Not automatically. The series equals the function exactly when the REMAINDER R_n(x) = f(x) - Pₙ(x) → 0 as n → ∞. The polynomials must close the entire gap in the limit; if a stubborn remainder persists, the series converges to something OTHER than f.

For the AP's functions, the remainder does vanish on the interval, and the standard series ARE their functions there: eˣ = Σxⁿ/n! for all x; sin x and cos x everywhere; 1/(1-x) = Σxⁿ on (-1, 1); ln(1+x) on (-1, 1]. These equalities license everything in the manipulation chapter — substituting, differentiating, and integrating the series IS doing those operations to the function.

The remainder is what the Lagrange bound measures: not whether it vanishes (it does, for exam functions), but HOW FAST — bounding R_n(x) for a fixed n quantifies the truncation error of stopping at Pₙ. Series-equals-function is the qualitative fact; the Lagrange bound is its quantitative engine.

The Taylor series itself is constructed exactly as the polynomial was — coefficients f^{(k)}(a)/k! — just never truncated. The five Maclaurin series of the last chapter are Taylor series; the polynomials were their truncations all along. This chapter measures the truncation; the next manipulates the full series.
key_terms: The untruncated Σ[f^{(k)}(a)/k!](x-a)ᵏ — equals f iff R_n → 0
R_n(x) = f(x) - Pₙ(x): the gap the polynomials must close
On the AP's functions, the equality holds — licensing manipulation
boxes: ap_alert

The standard series EQUAL their functions on their intervals — eˣ, sin, cos everywhere; geometric and ln on (-1, 1). This equality is what makes substitution and term-by-term calculus (next chapter) legal; it is assumed, not re-proven, on the exam.

sections.title: The Lagrange Error Bound
sections.subtitle: The formula and its M
sections.body:
The Lagrange error bound: if |f^{(n+1)}(t)| ≤ M for all t between the center a and the point x, then the remainder satisfies |R_n(x)| ≤ M·|x - a|^{n+1}/(n+1)!. The truncation error after the nth-degree polynomial is bounded by the NEXT term's shape — |x - a|^{n+1}/(n+1)! — scaled by M, a ceiling on the (n+1)st derivative across the interval.

The formula reads as 'the first omitted term, with the derivative replaced by its worst-case size.' Where the alternating bound used the actual next term, Lagrange uses M·(next power)/(next factorial) — applicable to ANY Taylor series, alternating or not. It is the universal error tool; the alternating bound is its sharper special case.

Choosing M is the bound's only real subtlety, and it is graded. M must exceed |f^{(n+1)}| EVERYWHERE between a and x — find the (n+1)st derivative's maximum magnitude on that interval. For eˣ approximating e^{0.5} with P₃: f⁗(t) = eˣ, maximized at the right end, so M = e^{0.5} < 2 (or e^{0.5} ≈ 1.65 — any valid upper bound works, and a clean over-estimate like 2 is encouraged). For sin/cos, all derivatives are bounded by 1: M = 1 always, the friendliest case.

Worked: bound the error of P₃ for eˣ at x = 0.5. |R₃| ≤ M·(0.5)⁴/4! with M = e^{0.5} ≤ 2: |R₃| ≤ 2·(0.0625)/24 ≈ 0.0052. The true error (1.6487 - 1.6458 ≈ 0.0029) sits under the bound ✓ — Lagrange over-estimates, as a guarantee must.
key_terms: |R_n| ≤ M|x-a|^{n+1}/(n+1)!: next term's shape, worst-case derivative
An upper bound on |f^{(n+1)}| across the whole interval [a, x]
All their derivatives bounded by 1: M = 1, the easy case
boxes: ap_alert

M must bound the (n+1)st derivative on the ENTIRE interval between center and point — not just at one endpoint. A clean over-estimate (M = 2 for eˣ near 0, M = 1 for any sin/cos) is safe and encouraged; the bound only needs to be valid, not tight.

sections.title: Tolerance Inversions
sections.subtitle: How many terms for the accuracy
sections.body:
The exam's standard Lagrange item inverts the bound: how many terms guarantee a target accuracy? Set the bound ≤ ε and solve for n. To approximate e^{0.5} within 0.001 with M = 2: demand 2·(0.5)^{n+1}/(n+1)! ≤ 0.001, and test n = 3, 4, 5 until it holds (n = 4: 2·(0.5)⁵/120 ≈ 0.00052 ✓). Factorials make the inequality un-solvable algebraically — TESTING successive n is the intended method, and stating the first n that works is the answer.

The testing discipline: compute the bound for increasing n, stop at the first below tolerance, report that polynomial degree. Show the values that fail and the one that passes — the failing-then-passing pair is the visible work the rubric rewards, exactly like the integral test's term-count inversions.

For sin and cos, M = 1 simplifies every inversion: 'approximate sin(0.3) within 10⁻⁶' demands (0.3)^{n+1}/(n+1)! ≤ 10⁻⁶, tested upward. The friendliness of M = 1 makes trig the inversion genre's gentlest client, and the exam favors it for clean arithmetic.

The inversion's cousin — fixed n, find the error — is the forward bound: 'bound the error of P₅ for cos(0.4)'. Both directions are one formula; reading which the question wants (count given, find error / accuracy given, find count) routes the computation. The forward direction computes once; the inverse tests upward.
key_terms: Bound ≤ ε, solve for n by testing successive degrees
Show the failing n and the passing n: the visible graded work
Fixed n → find error; fixed ε → find n by testing
boxes: ap_alert

Lagrange inversions can't be solved algebraically (factorials) — TEST successive n until the bound drops below tolerance, and show the work: 'n = 3 gives 0.004 > 0.001; n = 4 gives 0.0005 < 0.001, so 5 terms suffice.' The failing-passing pair is the rubric's evidence.

sections.title: Choosing the Error Tool
sections.subtitle: Lagrange vs alternating, and the FRQ's error part
sections.body:
Two error bounds, one decision. ALTERNATING bound (chapter 5): for an alternating series with decreasing magnitudes, |error| ≤ first omitted term — sharper, simpler, one term. LAGRANGE bound (here): for any Taylor series, |R_n| ≤ M|x-a|^{n+1}/(n+1)! — universal, requires choosing M. The rule: if the series at the evaluation point ALTERNATES with decreasing terms, use the alternating bound (it is tighter and faster); otherwise, Lagrange.

The routing in practice: sin(0.5), cos(0.5), e^{-0.5}, ln(1.3) all produce alternating series at those points — alternating bound, one term, done. By contrast e^{0.5} and e² give the all-positive eˣ series: NOT alternating, so Lagrange. The sign pattern at the SPECIFIC point decides, and checking it is the first move of any error part.

The FRQ's error part (part (c) of the standard Taylor FRQ) is where this routing pays: the exam writes the numbers so the intended bound is clean. An alternating evaluation point signals the alternating bound; an all-positive one signals Lagrange. Reaching for the harder tool when the easier applies is legal but loses time and invites M-choice errors.

The unit's error culture, complete: every approximation ships with a bound (the discipline from Unit 4's linearization, through the integral test's tails, to here). Series approximation without an error estimate is half an answer; the bound — alternating or Lagrange, correctly chosen and cited — is the other half, and the FRQ grades it as such.
key_terms: Alternating (sharp, alternating series only) vs Lagrange (universal, needs M)
Alternating at the point → alternating bound; all-positive → Lagrange
Every approximation carries a bound — the unit's through-line, completed
boxes: ap_alert

Check the series' sign pattern AT THE EVALUATION POINT before choosing the bound: sin(0.5), cos(0.5), e^{-0.5}, ln(1.2) alternate (use the alternating bound); e^{0.5}, e² do not (use Lagrange). The exam's numbers reward the right choice with clean arithmetic.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = eˣ, approximated near 0 by its third-degree Maclaurin polynomial P₃.
(a) Write P₃ and use it to estimate e^{0.4}.
(b) Use the Lagrange error bound to bound |e^{0.4} - P₃(0.4)|, justifying your choice of M.
(c) Determine the smallest degree n guaranteeing |e^{0.4} - Pₙ(0.4)| < 0.0001.
rubric: M justified; failing-passing pair shown for (c)

frq.question:
Approximate sin(0.6) using the Taylor (Maclaurin) series for sine.
(a) Write the series through the x⁵ term and compute the approximation using terms through x³.
(b) Since the series alternates at x = 0.6, bound the error of the x³-truncation using the ALTERNATING bound.
(c) Confirm the Lagrange bound (with M = 1) gives a valid but weaker estimate of the same error.
rubric: (c) Lagrange with n = 3, M = 1: (0.6)⁴/4! = 0.1296/24 = 0.0054 — valid, larger
Both bounds computed; alternating shown to be tighter
frq.model_answer: (a) sin x = x - x³/3! + x⁵/5! - ⋯ = x - x³/6 + x⁵/120 - ⋯. Through the x³ term: sin(0.6) ≈ 0.6 - (0.216)/6 = 0.6 - 0.036 = 0.564. (b) The series alternates with decreasing magnitudes at x = 0.6, so the error is at most the first omitted term, x⁵/120 = (0.6)⁵/120 ≈ 0.000648. (c) Lagrange with n = 3 and M = 1 (all sine derivatives bounded by 1): |R₃| ≤ 1·(0.6)⁴/4! = 0.1296/24 = 0.0054 — a valid bound, but about eight times looser than the alternating one. The alternating bound is sharper precisely because it uses the actual next term rather than a worst-case derivative; both certify the approximation, and the alternating bound is the intended tool here.

frq.question:
A function f satisfies |f^{(n)}(x)| ≤ n for all n and all x in [0, 2], and f and its derivatives at 0 are f(0) = 1, f'(0) = 1, f''(0) = 2.
(a) Write the second-degree Maclaurin polynomial P₂.
(b) Bound |f(1) - P₂(1)| using the Lagrange error bound with the given derivative ceiling.
(c) Explain why the bound from (b) guarantees P₂(1) approximates f(1) to within 1, and whether that is good enough to determine f(1) to the nearest integer.
rubric: (c) Error ≤ 1/2: P₂(1) = 3, so f(1) ∈ (2.5, 3.5) — determines the nearest integer as 3
Correct ceiling (M = 3 for the third derivative) selected
frq.model_answer: (a) P₂(x) = f(0) + f'(0)x + [f''(0)/2!]x² = 1 + x + (2/2)x² = 1 + x + x². (b) For P₂ the remainder uses the THIRD derivative: |f'''(x)| ≤ 3 on [0, 2] by the given bound (n = 3), so M = 3. |R₂(1)| ≤ M·|1|³/3! = 3/6 = 1/2. (c) The bound says |f(1) - P₂(1)| ≤ 1/2 — better than 1, so f(1) lies within 1/2 of P₂(1) = 3, i.e., in (2.5, 3.5). That interval contains exactly one integer, 3, so the approximation DOES determine f(1) to the nearest integer: f(1) rounds to 3.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: The course's finale: take a known series and substitute, differentiate, integrate, or multiply — and a new series for a new function appears, no derivatives computed. Five memorized series become a library of dozens, and the whole of calculus closes with power series doing what power series do best.
learning_objectives: Generate new series by substituting into known ones
Differentiate and integrate power series term by term
Derive the arctan and ln series from the geometric series
Multiply and add series for products and combinations
Use series to evaluate limits and otherwise-impossible integrals

sections.title: Substitution
sections.subtitle: New functions for free
sections.body:
The cheapest series-building move: substitute an expression for x in a known series. From eˣ = Σxⁿ/n!: replace x with -x for e^{-x} = Σ(-x)ⁿ/n! = 1 - x + x²/2! - ⋯; with x² for e^{x²} = 1 + x² + x⁴/2! + ⋯; with 2x for e^{2x} = Σ(2x)ⁿ/n!. Each substitution is exact and instantaneous — eight derivatives of e^{x²} replaced by one substitution (last chapter's coefficient trick, now systematized).

The interval transforms with the substitution: 1/(1-x) = Σxⁿ converges on (-1, 1), so 1/(1 + x²) = Σ(-x²)ⁿ = Σ(-1)ⁿx²ⁿ converges where |-x²| < 1, i.e., |x| < 1 — same interval here, but substituting 2x would halve it. Track the new radius by applying the original's condition to the substituted expression.

Trig substitutions multiply the library: sin(x²), cos(2x), e^{sin x} (first few terms) — all from the five base series. The move handles every 'find the Maclaurin series of [composite]' question without the derivative tower, and the AP asks these constantly because the substitution is the elegant route the exam rewards.

The discipline: substitute the WHOLE expression into every x, simplify powers, and keep enough terms for the question. e^{x²} through x⁶ needs the eˣ series through the cube (since (x²)³ = x⁶); reading how many base-series terms a target degree requires is the bookkeeping that keeps substitution honest.
key_terms: Replace x with an expression in a known series — exact, instant
Apply the original convergence condition to the substituted expression
Target degree determines how many base-series terms to carry
boxes: ap_alert

'Find the Maclaurin series of e^{x²}' (or sin(x²), 1/(1+x²)...) is a SUBSTITUTION problem — never compute derivatives. Replace x with the inside expression in the memorized series; the exam writes these expecting the one-line substitution, not the eight-derivative grind.

sections.title: Term-by-Term Calculus
sections.subtitle: Differentiate and integrate the series
sections.body:
Inside its interval of convergence, a power series can be differentiated and integrated TERM BY TERM, and the result is the series for the derivative or integral of the function. d/dx Σcₙxⁿ = Σncₙxⁿ⁻¹; ∫Σcₙxⁿ dx = Σcₙxⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C. The radius of convergence is preserved (endpoints may change). Calculus on functions becomes algebra on coefficients.

The consistency checks delight: differentiating sin's series x - x³/3! + x⁵/5! - ⋯ term by term gives 1 - x²/2! + x⁴/4! - ⋯ = cos's series ✓; differentiating eˣ's series returns itself ✓. The Maclaurin library is internally coherent under calculus — the series KNOW their functions' derivative relationships.

The headline derivations, both from the geometric series. ARCTAN: 1/(1 + x²) = Σ(-1)ⁿx²ⁿ (substitution); integrate term by term: arctan x = Σ(-1)ⁿx²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n+1) = x - x³/3 + x⁵/5 - ⋯. LN: 1/(1+x) = Σ(-x)ⁿ; integrate: ln(1+x) = x - x²/2 + x³/3 - ⋯ (last chapter's series, now DERIVED, not differentiated). Two famous series from one geometric seed plus an integral.

The arctan series at x = 1 yields the Leibniz formula π/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ⋯ — the thread from Unit 3's arctan derivative, promised there, arriving here: '1/(1+x²) → geometric series → term-by-term integration → π/4.' The course's longest single thread, tied off in the final chapter.
key_terms: Differentiate/integrate a power series coefficient by coefficient; radius preserved
sin' = cos and eˣ' = eˣ at the series level — the library is consistent
Substitute then integrate the geometric series for two famous series
boxes: ap_alert

The arctan and ln series are DERIVED from the geometric series by substitute-then-integrate — this derivation is a tested FRQ move. Starting from 1/(1+x²) or 1/(1+x), substituting, and integrating term by term is the expected work; memorizing the results is a backup, not a substitute for the method.

sections.title: Products, Sums, and the +C
sections.subtitle: Combining series carefully
sections.body:
Series add term by term: (eˣ + cos x)'s series sums the two coefficient-wise. Series multiply by distributing and COLLECTING like powers — eˣ·sin x through x³: (1 + x + x²/2 + ⋯)(x - x³/6 + ⋯) = x + x² + (1/2 - 1/6)x³ + ⋯ = x + x² + x³/3 + ⋯. Multiplication is finite bookkeeping when only the first few terms are wanted — gather each power's contributions, a polynomial-multiplication discipline.

The integration +C needs pinning, exactly as in Unit 6's IVPs. Deriving ln(1+x) by integrating Σ(-x)ⁿ gives Σ(-1)ⁿxⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C; the condition ln(1) = 0 (at x = 0) pins C = 0. Term-by-term integration produces a constant that an initial value resolves — skip it and the series is shifted wrong. The +C discipline, last seen integrating rates, returns for integrating series.

The product move's exam appetite is light (first few terms only), but the SUBSTITUTION-INTO-PRODUCT compositions appear: x·eˣ, x²cos x — multiply the base series by the monomial, shifting every power. x²cos x = x²(1 - x²/2 + ⋯) = x² - x⁴/2 + ⋯, a one-line shift. Monomial-times-series is the gentlest combination and a frequent FRQ component.

What combinations preserve: convergence on the INTERSECTION of the pieces' intervals (sums/products), and the radius under term-by-term calculus. The combined series is valid where all its ingredients are — a finite-head-style observation generalizing the convergence bookkeeping the unit has tracked throughout.
key_terms: Sum coefficient-wise; multiply by distributing and collecting like powers
Term-by-term integration's constant, pinned by an initial value
x^k times a series shifts every power up by k — the easy combination
boxes: ap_alert

When integrating a series term by term, the +C is real — pin it with a known value (usually f(0)). Deriving ln(1+x) from 1/(1+x), the constant is 0 because ln 1 = 0; forgetting to check shifts the entire series and the FRQ point with it.

sections.title: Series as a Calculus Tool
sections.subtitle: Limits, integrals, and the course's close
sections.body:
Power series solve problems other tools can't. INTEGRALS without elementary antiderivatives: ∫e^{x²}dx, ∫sin(x²)dx, ∫(sin x)/x dx — substitute the series, integrate term by term, and a series for the integral appears. ∫₀¹ e^{x²}dx = ∫₀¹(1 + x² + x⁴/2 + ⋯)dx = 1 + 1/3 + 1/10 + ⋯ — the BC-only definite integral that defeated Unit 6, now evaluable to any accuracy. The unit's improper-integral guests (e^{-x²} and friends) finally yield.

LIMITS that resist L'Hospital: lim x→0 (sin x - x)/x³. Substitute sine's series: (x - x³/6 + ⋯ - x)/x³ = (-x³/6 + ⋯)/x³ → -1/6. The series exposes the leading behavior directly — often faster than repeated L'Hospital, and immune to its differentiation grind. Series-for-limits is a genuine technique the exam occasionally rewards.

The combination move's payoff is the full series library: from five memorized series, substitution builds composites, calculus builds arctan/ln/integrals-of-the-unintegrable, and combination builds products and sums. The library is effectively unbounded — and every entry traces to eˣ, sin, cos, geometric, and ln by mechanical moves. This is the unit's, and the course's, final power.

The course closes here, and the threads tie off: derivatives (Units 2-3) became Taylor coefficients; integrals (Units 6, 8) became term-by-term operations; convergence (Unit 6's improper integrals) became series tests; approximation (Unit 4's linearization) became Taylor polynomials with Lagrange bounds; and arctan's derivative (Unit 3) became π/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ⋯. Calculus is one subject — limits, derivatives, integrals, and infinite sums, each the others in a different light — and the series unit is where the light reveals the whole.
key_terms: ∫e^{x²}, ∫sin(x²): substitute, integrate term by term — the unintegrable, integrated
Expose leading behavior directly: (sin x - x)/x³ → -1/6 in one line
Five base series + three moves = effectively every series the AP needs
boxes: ap_alert

∫₀^b e^{x²} dx and similar 'impossible' integrals are SERIES problems on the BC exam: substitute the Maclaurin series, integrate term by term, evaluate. The integral that had no antiderivative in Unit 6 becomes a numerical series here — the unit's grand payoff, and a guaranteed FRQ flavor.

frq.question:
Start from the geometric series 1/(1 - x) = Σₙ₌₀^∞ xⁿ, valid for |x| < 1.
(a) Find the Maclaurin series for 1/(1 + x²) by substitution, and its interval of convergence.
(b) Integrate term by term to obtain the series for arctan x, pinning the constant.
(c) Evaluate the series at x = 1 to express π in terms of an infinite series, and name the convergence behavior at that endpoint.
rubric: (b) Integrate: arctan x = Σ(-1)ⁿx²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n+1); arctan 0 = 0 pins C = 0
frq.model_answer: (a) Substituting -x² for x in the geometric series: 1/(1 + x²) = 1/(1 - (-x²)) = Σ(-x²)ⁿ = Σ(-1)ⁿx²ⁿ = 1 - x² + x⁴ - x⁶ + ⋯, converging where |-x²| < 1, i.e., |x| < 1. (b) Integrating term by term: arctan x = Σ(-1)ⁿx²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n+1) + C = x - x³/3 + x⁵/5 - ⋯ + C. At x = 0, arctan 0 = 0 forces C = 0: arctan x = x - x³/3 + x⁵/5 - ⋯. (c) At x = 1: arctan 1 = π/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ⋯ (the Leibniz formula), so π = 4(1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ⋯). At the endpoint x = 1 the series converges CONDITIONALLY — it alternates with magnitudes 1/(2n+1) decreasing to zero (AST), while the absolute series Σ1/(2n+1) diverges by comparison with the harmonic series.

frq.question:
Let g(x) = ∫₀ˣ e^{-t²} dt (the error-function shape, with no elementary antiderivative).
(a) Write the Maclaurin series for e^{-t²} and integrate term by term to find the series for g(x).
(b) Use the first three nonzero terms to approximate g(0.5).
(c) The series for g alternates at x = 0.5. Bound the error of your three-term approximation.
rubric: Term-by-term integration and alternating bound both shown
frq.model_answer: (a) e^{-t²} = 1 - t² + t⁴/2! - t⁶/3! + ⋯ (substitute -t² into eˣ). Integrate from 0 to x term by term: g(x) = x - x³/3 + x⁵/(5·2) - x⁷/(7·6) + ⋯ = x - x³/3 + x⁵/10 - x⁷/42 + ⋯. (b) First three nonzero terms at x = 0.5: 0.5 - (0.5)³/3 + (0.5)⁵/10 = 0.5 - 0.125/3 + 0.03125/10 = 0.5 - 0.04167 + 0.003125 ≈ 0.46146. (c) The series alternates with decreasing magnitudes at 0.5, so the error is at most the first omitted term: (0.5)⁷/42 = 0.0078125/42 ≈ 0.000186. The approximation 0.46146 is within 0.0002 of the true g(0.5).

frq.question:
Use Maclaurin series to evaluate the limit and the integral.
(a) Evaluate lim x→0 (1 - cos x)/x² using the cosine series.
(b) Evaluate lim x→0 (x - sin x)/x³ similarly.
(c) Write the first three nonzero terms of the series for x cos x, and use it to set up ∫₀¹ x cos x dx as a numerical series (do not sum).
rubric: (b) x - sin x = x³/6 - x⁵/120 + ⋯; over x³: 1/6 - x²/120 → 1/6
Series substitution shown for each; integral assembled term by term
frq.model_answer: (a) cos x = 1 - x²/2! + x⁴/4! - ⋯, so 1 - cos x = x²/2 - x⁴/24 + ⋯. Dividing by x²: 1/2 - x²/24 + ⋯ → 1/2 as x → 0. (b) sin x = x - x³/6 + x⁵/120 - ⋯, so x - sin x = x³/6 - x⁵/120 + ⋯. Over x³: 1/6 - x²/120 + ⋯ → 1/6. (c) x cos x = x(1 - x²/2 + x⁴/24 - ⋯) = x - x³/2 + x⁵/24 - ⋯. Integrating from 0 to 1 term by term: ∫₀¹ x cos x dx = [x²/2 - x⁴/8 + x⁶/144 - ⋯]₀¹ = 1/2 - 1/8 + 1/144 - ⋯ — the impossible-looking integral rendered as a clean numerical series, the unit's closing trick. (Its exact value, cos 1 + sin 1 - 1 by parts, confirms the series ≈ 0.3818.)
